data.objective: Observe the global macroeconomic and monetary environment and identify meaningful changes in growth, inflation, employment, liquidity, interest rates, and central-bank policy.
data.initialContextTokenization: Estimated with the local gpt-4o tokenizer; foundational context only.

indicator.name: Federal Funds Rate
indicator.description: The effective interest rate at which U.S. depository institutions lend federal funds to one another overnight. It is a market-determined rate influenced by the Federal Reserve's monetary policy framework and target range.
indicator.use: Monitor the stance and transmission of U.S. monetary policy and assess changes in short-term interest rates, liquidity, financial conditions, and broader economic activity.
indicator.purpose: Provide a core measure of short-term U.S. interest rates for monetary policy analysis, financial condition analysis, and cross-indicator interpretation within the intelligence system.
indicator.significance: The federal funds rate is a central short-term interest rate in the U.S. financial system. Changes in the rate influence other short-term rates and indirectly affect borrowing costs, financial conditions, economic activity, and asset markets.

indicator.name: Federal Reserve Total Assets
indicator.description: The total assets held by the Federal Reserve, reported as a weekly level measured as of Wednesday and expressed in millions of U.S. dollars. The series is not seasonally adjusted.
indicator.use: Monitor changes in the size of the Federal Reserve's balance sheet and assess shifts in monetary liquidity and central-bank asset holdings.
indicator.purpose: Provide a broad measure of Federal Reserve total assets for analyzing balance-sheet policy, liquidity conditions, quantitative easing or tightening, and changes in the U.S. monetary environment.
indicator.significance: Federal Reserve total assets provide a high-frequency measure of the size of the central bank's balance sheet. Changes can reflect movements in securities holdings, lending facilities, and other Federal Reserve assets and can therefore provide context for changes in monetary and financial conditions.

indicator.name: Reserve Balances
indicator.description: The average level of reserve balances held by depository institutions at Federal Reserve Banks during the week ending Wednesday. The series is not seasonally adjusted and is reported in millions of U.S. dollars.
indicator.use: Monitor the level of reserve balances held by depository institutions at Federal Reserve Banks and assess changes in banking-system liquidity and monetary conditions.
indicator.purpose: Provide a measure of reserve balances within the U.S. banking system for analyzing Federal Reserve balance-sheet operations, liquidity conditions, and the implementation of monetary policy.
indicator.significance: Reserve balances represent funds that depository institutions hold at Federal Reserve Banks. Changes in reserve balances provide information about banking-system liquidity and can help interpret the effects of Federal Reserve balance-sheet operations and broader monetary conditions.

indicator.name: Reverse Repo Usage
indicator.description: The aggregated daily amount of overnight reverse repurchase agreement transactions conducted by the Federal Reserve with eligible counterparties. The series is not seasonally adjusted and is reported in billions of U.S. dollars.
indicator.use: Monitor usage of the Federal Reserve's overnight reverse repurchase facility and assess changes in short-term liquidity and money-market conditions.
indicator.purpose: Provide a measure of overnight reverse repo activity for analyzing Federal Reserve open-market operations, money-market liquidity, reserve conditions, and changes in short-term financial conditions.
indicator.significance: Reverse repo usage reflects the amount of funds placed into the Federal Reserve's overnight reverse repurchase facility by eligible counterparties. Changes in usage can provide information about money-market conditions, the distribution of liquidity, and the interaction between Federal Reserve operations and short-term interest rates.

indicator.name: M2 Money Supply
indicator.description: A broad measure of the U.S. money supply consisting of currency and deposits and other liquid assets included in the Federal Reserve's M2 monetary aggregate. The series is seasonally adjusted and reported in billions of dollars.
indicator.use: Monitor changes in the quantity of money circulating through the U.S. financial system and assess changes in liquidity and monetary conditions.
indicator.purpose: Provide a broad measure of the U.S. money supply for analyzing monetary conditions, liquidity, financial activity, and relationships between money growth and broader economic conditions.
indicator.significance: M2 provides a broad measure of money and liquid deposits available within the U.S. financial system. Changes in M2 can provide information about shifts in monetary and liquidity conditions and can be analyzed alongside inflation, interest rates, credit, and economic activity.

indicator.name: Consumer Price Index
indicator.description: A seasonally adjusted price index measuring changes in the prices paid by urban consumers for a broad basket of goods and services in the United States. The index is based on a reference period of 1982–1984 = 100.
indicator.use: Monitor changes in consumer prices and assess inflation and deflation across the broad basket of goods and services purchased by urban consumers.
indicator.purpose: Provide a broad measure of changes in consumer prices for analyzing inflation trends, purchasing power, monetary policy, and economic conditions.
indicator.significance: The CPI is one of the primary measures used to monitor consumer price changes in the U.S. Changes in the index can indicate shifts in inflationary or deflationary conditions and are relevant to monetary policy, household purchasing power, and economic analysis.

indicator.name: Core Consumer Price Index
indicator.description: A seasonally adjusted price index measuring changes in the prices paid by urban consumers for a broad basket of goods and services, excluding food and energy. The index uses a reference period of 1982–1984 = 100.
indicator.use: Monitor underlying consumer price trends while reducing the influence of the relatively volatile food and energy components.
indicator.purpose: Provide a measure of underlying consumer price movements for analyzing persistent inflation trends, monetary policy, and broader economic conditions.
indicator.significance: Core CPI is widely used in economic analysis because excluding food and energy can reduce the influence of short-term volatility in those components. Changes in core prices provide information about broader and potentially more persistent consumer price pressures.

indicator.name: Personal Consumption Expenditures
indicator.description: A measure of spending by households on goods and services in the United States. The series is reported as a seasonally adjusted annual rate and expressed in billions of dollars.
indicator.use: Monitor household consumption and changes in consumer spending, a major component of U.S. economic activity.
indicator.purpose: Provide a broad measure of personal consumption expenditures for analyzing consumer demand, economic growth, household spending behavior, and broader economic conditions.
indicator.significance: Personal consumption expenditures represent a major component of U.S. economic activity. Changes in consumer spending can provide information about household demand, economic momentum, and shifts in consumption patterns.

indicator.name: Core PCE Price Index
indicator.description: A seasonally adjusted price index measuring changes in the prices paid for goods and services in the United States, excluding food and energy. The index is a chain-type measure with a reference period of 2017 = 100.
indicator.use: Monitor underlying consumer price trends while reducing the influence of volatile food and energy prices.
indicator.purpose: Provide a broad measure of underlying consumer inflation for analyzing persistent price pressures, monetary policy, inflation expectations, and economic conditions.
indicator.significance: The Core PCE Price Index is a major measure of underlying consumer price inflation in the United States. Excluding food and energy reduces the influence of volatile components and provides a broader measure of underlying price trends. The index is also used in macroeconomic analysis and monetary policy assessment.

indicator.name: 5-Year Breakeven Inflation Rate
indicator.description: A market-based measure of expected average inflation over the next five years, derived from the difference between 5-year nominal Treasury yields and 5-year inflation-indexed Treasury yields.
indicator.use: Monitor market-based inflation expectations over a five-year horizon and identify changes in the outlook for future inflation.
indicator.purpose: Provide a market-derived measure of expected average inflation over the next five years for analyzing inflation expectations, monetary policy, Treasury markets, and financial conditions.
indicator.significance: The 5-year breakeven inflation rate reflects inflation expectations implied by the relative pricing of nominal and inflation-indexed Treasury securities. Changes in the measure can provide information about shifts in market expectations for medium-term inflation.

indicator.name: 10-Year Breakeven Inflation Rate
indicator.description: A market-based measure of expected average inflation over the next ten years, derived from the difference between nominal 10-year Treasury yields and 10-year Treasury inflation-indexed securities.
indicator.use: Monitor market-based inflation expectations and changes in the outlook for long-term inflation.
indicator.purpose: Provide a market-derived measure of expected average inflation over a ten-year horizon for analyzing inflation expectations, Treasury markets, monetary policy, and financial conditions.
indicator.significance: The 10-year breakeven inflation rate reflects the inflation compensation implied by the pricing difference between nominal and inflation-indexed Treasury securities. Changes in the measure can provide information about shifts in market-based inflation expectations.

indicator.name: Producer Price Index
indicator.description: A monthly price index measuring changes in prices received by producers across all commodities in the United States. The index uses a reference period of 1982 = 100 and is not seasonally adjusted.
indicator.use: Monitor changes in prices received by producers across the broad commodity economy and assess producer-level price pressures.
indicator.purpose: Provide a broad measure of producer price movements for analyzing upstream inflation pressures, commodity pricing, production costs, and potential changes in consumer prices.
indicator.significance: The Producer Price Index provides information about price changes at the producer level before goods and services reach consumers. Changes in producer prices can provide insight into upstream inflation pressures and changes in production costs.

indicator.name: Nonfarm Payrolls
indicator.description: The number of employees in the U.S. nonfarm economy, excluding proprietors, private household employees, unpaid volunteers, farm employees, and the unincorporated self-employed. The series is seasonally adjusted and reported in thousands of persons.
indicator.use: Monitor changes in total nonfarm employment and assess labor-market conditions, job creation, and changes in overall economic activity.
indicator.purpose: Provide a broad measure of U.S. employment for analyzing labor-market strength, economic growth, household income, business activity, and changes in the business cycle.
indicator.significance: Nonfarm payrolls are a major measure of U.S. employment and provide information about changes in the number of jobs across the economy. Sustained increases or decreases can provide insight into labor-market conditions and broader economic momentum.

indicator.name: Unemployment Rate
indicator.description: The percentage of the U.S. civilian labor force that is unemployed. This series represents the U-3 measure of labor underutilization and is seasonally adjusted.
indicator.use: Monitor labor market conditions and changes in the share of the labor force that is unemployed.
indicator.purpose: Provide a core measure of U.S. labor market conditions for analyzing employment, economic activity, monetary policy, household conditions, and changes in the business cycle.
indicator.significance: The unemployment rate is a widely used measure of labor market conditions and economic slack. Changes in unemployment can provide information about labor-market strength, household income conditions, economic activity, and the broader business cycle.

indicator.name: Initial Jobless Claims
indicator.description: The number of initial claims for unemployment insurance filed by individuals following separation from an employer. The series is seasonally adjusted and reported weekly, with observations representing the week ending Saturday.
indicator.use: Monitor new unemployment insurance claims and identify changes in labor-market conditions, layoffs, and emerging weakness or strength in employment.
indicator.purpose: Provide a high-frequency measure of new unemployment insurance claims for analyzing labor-market conditions and detecting changes in employment trends before slower monthly indicators are released.
indicator.significance: Initial jobless claims provide a timely signal of new unemployment following job separations. Sustained changes in claims can provide information about labor-market conditions, layoffs, and shifts in economic activity.

indicator.name: Job Openings
indicator.description: The number of available nonfarm jobs that remain unfilled on the last business day of the month and meet the criteria for an active job opening. The series is seasonally adjusted and reported in thousands of job openings.
indicator.use: Monitor unmet demand for labor and changes in the availability of job opportunities across the nonfarm economy.
indicator.purpose: Provide a measure of labor demand and job-market tightness for analyzing employment conditions, labor shortages, hiring demand, and changes in economic activity.
indicator.significance: Job openings provide information about demand for workers that has not yet been met through hiring. Changes in openings can indicate shifts in labor-market tightness, employer hiring demand, and the balance between available workers and available jobs.

indicator.name: Labor Force Participation Rate
indicator.description: The percentage of the civilian noninstitutional population that is either employed or actively looking for work. The series is seasonally adjusted and published monthly.
indicator.use: Monitor changes in labor-force participation and assess shifts in the share of the population engaged in the labor market.
indicator.purpose: Provide a core measure of labor-force engagement for analyzing labor-market conditions, economic activity, workforce availability, and longer-term demographic and economic trends.
indicator.significance: The labor force participation rate provides information about the share of the population working or actively seeking work. Changes in participation can affect the available labor supply and help distinguish changes in unemployment from changes in labor-force entry or exit.

indicator.name: Average Hourly Earnings
indicator.description: The average gross hourly earnings of all private-sector employees in the United States, including premium pay for overtime and late-shift work. The series is seasonally adjusted and reported in dollars per hour.
indicator.use: Monitor changes in average hourly earnings and assess wage pressures, household income conditions, labor-market trends, and potential inflationary pressures.
indicator.purpose: Provide a broad measure of average hourly earnings in the private sector for analyzing labor-market conditions, wage growth, household income, inflation pressures, and economic activity.
indicator.significance: Average hourly earnings provide information about changes in the average hourly compensation received by private-sector workers. Changes can help identify wage pressures and their potential relationship with consumer spending and inflation, although movements can also reflect changes in the composition of workers rather than changes in individual workers' earnings.

indicator.name: Real Gross Domestic Product
indicator.description: The inflation-adjusted value of goods and services produced by labor and property located in the United States. The series is seasonally adjusted at an annual rate and reported in billions of chained 2017 dollars.
indicator.use: Monitor the inflation-adjusted level of U.S. economic output and assess changes in overall economic activity and growth.
indicator.purpose: Provide a broad measure of real U.S. economic output for analyzing economic growth, business-cycle conditions, productivity, and changes in aggregate economic activity.
indicator.significance: Real GDP measures the inflation-adjusted value of goods and services produced in the U.S. economy. Changes in real GDP provide a broad measure of economic expansion or contraction and are central to assessing overall economic conditions and the business cycle.

indicator.name: Real GDP Growth
indicator.description: The quarterly percentage change in inflation-adjusted U.S. gross domestic product from the preceding period, reported at an annual rate. The series is seasonally adjusted and measures changes in real economic output.
indicator.use: Monitor the pace of change in inflation-adjusted U.S. economic output and identify periods of economic expansion, slowing growth, or contraction.
indicator.purpose: Provide a published measure of quarterly real GDP growth for analyzing economic momentum, business-cycle conditions, and changes in aggregate economic activity.
indicator.significance: Real GDP growth measures changes in inflation-adjusted economic output and provides a broad indicator of economic momentum. Changes in the growth rate can help identify shifts between stronger and weaker periods of economic activity and changes in the business cycle.

indicator.name: Industrial Production
indicator.description: A seasonally adjusted index measuring the real output of the U.S. industrial sector, including manufacturing, mining, and electric and gas utilities. The index uses a reference period of 2017 = 100.
indicator.use: Monitor changes in U.S. industrial output and assess conditions across manufacturing, mining, and utility production.
indicator.purpose: Provide a broad measure of industrial-sector activity for analyzing economic momentum, production trends, business conditions, and changes in the business cycle.
indicator.significance: Industrial production provides information about real output in major industrial sectors of the U.S. economy. Changes in the index can help identify shifts in production activity and economic momentum, particularly within manufacturing and other industrial sectors.

indicator.name: Retail Sales
indicator.description: Seasonally adjusted monthly sales for U.S. retail trade and food services, reported in millions of dollars. The most recent observation is an advance estimate based on a subsample of firms and is subject to revision.
indicator.use: Monitor consumer spending activity through changes in retail trade and food-service sales and identify shifts in consumer demand and economic momentum.
indicator.purpose: Provide a timely measure of nominal retail and food-service sales for analyzing consumer demand, household spending, economic activity, and changes in consumption trends.
indicator.significance: Retail sales provide a timely signal of consumer demand and economic activity. Changes in sales can indicate shifts in household spending behavior and economic momentum, although the latest observation is an advance estimate and may be revised as more complete survey data become available.

indicator.name: Personal Income
indicator.description: The income received by individuals in the United States from labor, property, and capital, together with net current transfer payments received from businesses and government. The series is reported as a seasonally adjusted annual rate in billions of dollars.
indicator.use: Monitor changes in aggregate income received by households and assess household financial conditions, consumer spending capacity, and economic activity.
indicator.purpose: Provide a broad measure of personal income for analyzing household income conditions, consumer demand, savings, and changes in overall economic activity.
indicator.significance: Personal income captures income received by individuals from labor, assets, and transfers. Changes in personal income can provide information about household purchasing capacity and economic conditions and can help explain changes in consumer spending.

indicator.name: Consumer Sentiment
indicator.description: The University of Michigan Consumer Sentiment Index, a survey-based measure of U.S. consumer attitudes and expectations regarding economic conditions. The index uses a reference period of 1966 Q1 = 100, is not seasonally adjusted, and is reported monthly.
indicator.use: Monitor changes in consumer attitudes and expectations about economic conditions and assess shifts in household confidence and sentiment.
indicator.purpose: Provide a survey-based measure of consumer sentiment for analyzing household expectations, consumer behavior, economic conditions, and potential changes in consumer spending.
indicator.significance: Consumer sentiment provides information about how households perceive current and expected economic conditions. Changes in sentiment can help contextualize consumer spending and economic activity, although sentiment reflects survey responses and does not directly measure realized household behavior. The source data is delayed by one month at the request of the University of Michigan.

indicator.name: Building Permits
indicator.description: The number of new privately owned housing units authorized by building permits in permit-issuing places across the United States. The series is reported monthly as a seasonally adjusted annual rate and expressed in thousands of units.
indicator.use: Monitor authorized residential construction activity and assess changes in housing demand, construction intentions, and conditions in the housing market.
indicator.purpose: Provide a timely measure of new residential building permits for analyzing prospective construction activity, housing-market conditions, construction investment, and the effects of interest rates and financial conditions on housing demand.
indicator.significance: Building permits provide information about residential construction that has been authorized but may not yet have begun. Changes in permits can provide insight into prospective construction activity, builder intentions, housing demand, and the broader economic cycle.

indicator.name: Housing Starts
indicator.description: The number of new privately owned housing units started in the United States, where a start occurs when excavation begins for the footings or foundation of a building. The series is reported monthly as a seasonally adjusted annual rate and expressed in thousands of units.
indicator.use: Monitor new residential construction activity and assess changes in housing-sector conditions, construction demand, economic activity, and sensitivity to financing conditions.
indicator.purpose: Provide a timely measure of residential construction starts for analyzing housing-market activity, construction investment, economic growth, and the effects of interest rates and financial conditions on housing demand.
indicator.significance: Housing starts provide information about new residential construction activity and are an important component of the housing and construction sectors. Changes in starts can provide insight into builders' activity, housing demand, construction investment, and the broader economic cycle.

indicator.name: Existing Home Sales
indicator.description: The volume of transactions involving existing single-family homes, condominiums, and cooperative housing units in the United States. The series is reported monthly as a seasonally adjusted annual rate and expressed as the number of units.
indicator.use: Monitor activity in the existing residential housing market and assess changes in home-buying demand, housing-market turnover, and broader economic conditions.
indicator.purpose: Provide a measure of existing-home transaction volume for analyzing housing-market activity, household demand, market turnover, and the relationship between housing conditions and the broader economy.
indicator.significance: Existing-home sales measure the volume of transactions for homes that were previously owned and occupied. Changes in sales activity can provide information about housing demand, market liquidity, affordability conditions, and household behavior, although transaction volume can also be affected by housing inventory and financing conditions.

indicator.name: U.S. National Home Price Index
indicator.description: The S&P Cotality Case-Shiller U.S. National Home Price Index, a monthly measure of U.S. residential property values based on repeat-sales pricing of existing single-family homes. The index is not seasonally adjusted and uses January 2000 = 100 as its reference period.
indicator.use: Monitor changes in U.S. residential property values and assess trends in home prices, housing-market conditions, household wealth, and housing affordability.
indicator.purpose: Provide a broad measure of national U.S. home-price levels for analyzing housing-market trends, changes in property values, household wealth, and relationships between housing prices, financing costs, income, and economic conditions.
indicator.significance: The national home price index provides information about changes in residential property values across the United States. Changes in home prices can affect housing affordability, household wealth, housing demand, construction incentives, and broader economic conditions.

indicator.name: 30-Year Fixed Mortgage Rate
indicator.description: The average interest rate for 30-year fixed-rate mortgages in the United States, based on Freddie Mac's weekly Primary Mortgage Market Survey. The rate is reported weekly for the period ending Thursday and is not seasonally adjusted.
indicator.use: Monitor mortgage financing costs and assess how changes in interest rates affect housing affordability, home-buying demand, refinancing activity, and residential construction.
indicator.purpose: Provide a high-frequency measure of U.S. 30-year fixed mortgage rates for analyzing housing-market conditions, household financing costs, interest-rate transmission, and the relationship between monetary and financial conditions and residential activity.
indicator.significance: Mortgage rates directly affect the financing cost of home purchases and refinancing. Changes in 30-year fixed mortgage rates can influence housing affordability, buyer demand, transaction activity, construction incentives, and the broader transmission of interest-rate conditions into the housing market.

indicator.name: 3-Month Treasury Bill Rate
indicator.description: The secondary market interest rate for U.S. Treasury bills with a three-month maturity, quoted on a discount basis. The series is reported daily and is not seasonally adjusted.
indicator.use: Monitor short-term U.S. Treasury interest rates and assess changes in money-market conditions, monetary policy expectations, and short-term government borrowing costs.
indicator.purpose: Provide a high-frequency measure of the three-month Treasury bill rate for analyzing short-term interest rates, monetary policy transmission, liquidity conditions, and the front end of the U.S. yield curve.
indicator.significance: The three-month Treasury bill rate is a key short-term interest-rate benchmark and reflects market pricing for very short-term U.S. government debt. Changes in the rate can provide information about short-term monetary and financial conditions and expectations surrounding Federal Reserve policy.

indicator.name: 2-Year Treasury Yield
indicator.description: The market yield on U.S. Treasury securities with a constant maturity of two years, quoted on an investment basis. It reflects market expectations and pricing for short-term U.S. government borrowing.
indicator.use: Monitor short-term U.S. interest rates, Treasury market conditions, monetary policy expectations, and changes in the cost of government borrowing.
indicator.purpose: Provide a market-based measure of the two-year point on the U.S. Treasury yield curve for analyzing interest-rate expectations, monetary policy, financial conditions, and relationships across the yield curve.
indicator.significance: The two-year Treasury yield is closely connected to expectations for future monetary policy and short-term interest rates. Changes in the yield can provide information about shifts in interest-rate expectations and broader financial conditions.

indicator.name: 5-Year Treasury Yield
indicator.description: The market yield on U.S. Treasury securities with a constant maturity of five years, quoted on an investment basis. The series is reported daily and is not seasonally adjusted.
indicator.use: Monitor intermediate-term U.S. Treasury interest rates and assess changes in market expectations, monetary policy transmission, inflation expectations, and broader financial conditions.
indicator.purpose: Provide a market-based measure of the five-year point on the U.S. Treasury yield curve for analyzing intermediate-term interest rates, economic expectations, monetary policy, and changes in financial conditions.
indicator.significance: The five-year Treasury yield reflects market pricing for intermediate-term U.S. government borrowing and incorporates expectations about future interest rates, inflation, and economic conditions. Changes in the yield can provide information about shifts in the middle portion of the Treasury yield curve and broader financial-market expectations.

indicator.name: 10-Year Treasury Yield
indicator.description: The market yield on U.S. Treasury securities with a constant maturity of ten years, quoted on an investment basis. It reflects market pricing for longer-term U.S. government borrowing and expectations about future economic and financial conditions.
indicator.use: Monitor long-term U.S. interest rates, Treasury market conditions, financial conditions, inflation and growth expectations, and changes in the cost of government borrowing.
indicator.purpose: Provide a market-based measure of the ten-year point on the U.S. Treasury yield curve for analyzing long-term interest rates, economic expectations, monetary policy transmission, and financial market conditions.
indicator.significance: The 10-year Treasury yield is a major benchmark for U.S. long-term interest rates and influences pricing across financial markets. Changes in the yield can reflect shifts in expectations for inflation, economic growth, monetary policy, and demand for government securities.

indicator.name: Real 10-Year Treasury Yield
indicator.description: The market yield on 10-year U.S. Treasury securities whose principal and interest payments are adjusted for inflation. It represents a market-based measure of the real interest rate for a 10-year maturity.
indicator.use: Monitor real long-term interest rates and assess changes in inflation-adjusted borrowing costs, financial conditions, and market expectations.
indicator.purpose: Provide a market-based measure of the real 10-year U.S. interest rate for analyzing real borrowing costs, inflation-adjusted returns, monetary policy, and financial conditions.
indicator.significance: The real 10-year Treasury yield provides information about the inflation-adjusted cost of long-term capital and the pricing of inflation-indexed government securities. Changes in the yield can affect financial conditions and the relative attractiveness of real versus nominal assets.

indicator.name: Nominal Broad U.S. Dollar Index
indicator.description: A trade-weighted index measuring the value of the U.S. dollar against a broad group of foreign currencies. The index is reported daily, is not seasonally adjusted, and uses January 2006 = 100 as its reference period.
indicator.use: Monitor changes in the broad nominal value of the U.S. dollar and assess foreign-exchange conditions, international financial conditions, trade competitiveness, and cross-border capital flows.
indicator.purpose: Provide a broad measure of U.S. dollar strength against major trading-partner currencies for analyzing foreign-exchange conditions, monetary policy transmission, global financial conditions, and relationships between the dollar and other asset markets.
indicator.significance: The broad U.S. dollar index provides a trade-weighted measure of changes in the dollar's value across a broad set of foreign currencies. Changes in the index can affect import prices, export competitiveness, international capital flows, commodity pricing, and global financial conditions.

indicator.name: Nominal Advanced Foreign Economies U.S. Dollar Index
indicator.description: A trade-weighted index measuring the nominal value of the U.S. dollar against currencies of advanced foreign economies. The index is reported daily, is not seasonally adjusted, and uses January 2006 = 100 as its reference period.
indicator.use: Monitor changes in the U.S. dollar's nominal value against currencies of advanced foreign economies and assess exchange-rate conditions, international financial conditions, and cross-border economic relationships.
indicator.purpose: Provide a trade-weighted measure of the U.S. dollar against advanced-economy currencies for analyzing foreign-exchange conditions, relative currency movements, monetary policy transmission, and international financial conditions.
indicator.significance: The index isolates movements in the U.S. dollar relative to currencies of advanced foreign economies using trade-weighted exchange rates. Changes can provide information about dollar strength, international capital conditions, trade relationships, and differences in monetary and economic conditions across major advanced economies.

indicator.name: Nominal Emerging Market Economies U.S. Dollar Index
indicator.description: A trade-weighted index measuring the nominal value of the U.S. dollar against currencies of emerging market economies. The index is reported daily, is not seasonally adjusted, and uses January 2006 = 100 as its reference period.
indicator.use: Monitor changes in the U.S. dollar's nominal value against currencies of emerging market economies and assess foreign-exchange conditions, global financial conditions, capital flows, and international economic relationships.
indicator.purpose: Provide a trade-weighted measure of the U.S. dollar against emerging-market currencies for analyzing foreign-exchange conditions, international financial conditions, monetary policy transmission, and changes in cross-border capital flows.
indicator.significance: The index measures movements in the U.S. dollar relative to currencies of emerging market economies using trade-weighted exchange rates. Changes in the index can provide information about dollar strength, emerging-market financial conditions, international capital flows, and differences in monetary and economic conditions across emerging markets.

indicator.name: High Yield Credit Spread
indicator.description: The ICE BofA U.S. High Yield Index Option-Adjusted Spread, measuring the spread between below-investment-grade U.S. corporate bonds and a comparable Treasury yield curve after adjusting for embedded options. The series is reported as a daily closing value and is not seasonally adjusted.
indicator.use: Monitor credit-market conditions and changes in the compensation investors demand for holding below-investment-grade corporate debt relative to U.S. Treasury securities.
indicator.purpose: Provide a market-based measure of high-yield corporate credit spreads for analyzing credit risk, financial conditions, investor risk pricing, and changes in stress across corporate bond markets.
indicator.significance: The high-yield credit spread reflects the additional yield demanded by investors for below-investment-grade corporate debt relative to a Treasury reference curve. Changes in the spread can provide information about shifts in perceived credit risk, risk appetite, and broader financial-market conditions.

indicator.name: Investment Grade Credit Spread
indicator.description: The ICE BofA U.S. Corporate Index Option-Adjusted Spread, measuring the spread between investment-grade U.S. corporate bonds and a comparable Treasury yield curve after adjusting for embedded options. The series is reported as a daily closing value and is not seasonally adjusted.
indicator.use: Monitor credit-market conditions and changes in the compensation investors demand for holding investment-grade corporate debt relative to U.S. Treasury securities.
indicator.purpose: Provide a market-based measure of investment-grade corporate credit spreads for analyzing credit risk, financial conditions, investor risk pricing, and changes in corporate bond markets.
indicator.significance: The investment-grade credit spread reflects the additional yield demanded by investors for investment-grade corporate debt relative to a Treasury reference curve. Changes in the spread can provide information about shifts in perceived credit risk, risk appetite, and broader financial-market conditions.

indicator.name: S&P 500
indicator.description: A market-capitalization-weighted index of 500 leading publicly traded U.S. companies across major industries, representing a broad measure of the large-cap U.S. equity market. The series is reported as a daily closing index value and is not seasonally adjusted.
indicator.use: Monitor broad U.S. equity-market performance and assess changes in investor risk appetite, financial conditions, market expectations, and the valuation of large-cap U.S. companies.
indicator.purpose: Provide a broad benchmark for U.S. large-cap equity markets for analyzing financial-market conditions, risk sentiment, economic expectations, and relationships between equity markets and macroeconomic indicators.
indicator.significance: The S&P 500 is a widely followed benchmark for the U.S. large-cap equity market. Changes in the index provide information about equity-market performance and investor expectations and can help contextualize broader financial conditions and risk sentiment. The series is a price index and does not include dividends or represent total return.

indicator.name: NASDAQ Composite
indicator.description: A market-capitalization-weighted index tracking more than 3,000 common equities listed on the NASDAQ Stock Market, including common stocks, American depositary receipts, real estate investment trusts, and tracking stocks. The series is reported as a daily closing index value and is not seasonally adjusted.
indicator.use: Monitor broad U.S. equity-market performance across companies listed on the NASDAQ and assess changes in market sentiment, risk appetite, and the performance of growth-oriented and technology-heavy segments of the equity market.
indicator.purpose: Provide a broad benchmark for NASDAQ-listed equities for analyzing equity-market conditions, investor risk appetite, market expectations, and changes across technology and growth-oriented portions of the U.S. stock market.
indicator.significance: The NASDAQ Composite provides broad exposure to equities listed on the NASDAQ Stock Market and includes companies across multiple industries, with substantial representation from technology and growth-oriented businesses. Changes in the index provide information about equity-market performance and investor expectations and can help contextualize broader financial-market conditions.

indicator.name: CBOE Volatility Index
indicator.description: A market-based measure of expected near-term volatility in U.S. stock markets derived from stock index option prices. The series is reported as a daily closing index value and is not seasonally adjusted.
indicator.use: Monitor changes in market-implied expectations for near-term equity-market volatility and identify shifts in financial-market uncertainty and risk conditions.
indicator.purpose: Provide a market-based measure of expected near-term stock-market volatility for analyzing investor risk expectations, market stress, financial conditions, and changes in market sentiment.
indicator.significance: The VIX reflects volatility expectations implied by stock index option prices. Changes in the index provide information about shifts in expected near-term equity-market volatility and can help contextualize changes in broader financial-market risk conditions.

indicator.name: AAII Investor Sentiment Survey
indicator.description: A weekly survey of individual investors measuring the percentage who expect the U.S. stock market to rise, remain essentially unchanged, or fall over the next six months. The dataset includes bullish, neutral, bearish, and bull-bear spread readings.
indicator.use: Monitor changes in individual-investor expectations, optimism, pessimism, uncertainty, and overall sentiment toward the U.S. stock market, including changes in the bull-bear spread.
indicator.purpose: Provide a direct survey-based measure of individual-investor expectations that complements market-derived sentiment indicators by capturing what retail investors expect the stock market to do over the following six months.
indicator.significance: The AAII Sentiment Survey provides a direct measure of individual-investor expectations rather than inferring sentiment from market prices or positioning. Changes in bullish, neutral, and bearish responses reveal shifts in optimism, pessimism, and uncertainty, while the bull-bear spread summarizes the balance between optimistic and pessimistic views. Extreme sentiment readings can provide useful context for assessing investor psychology and potential sentiment reversals, but the survey does not establish the future direction of the market.

indicator.name: CNN Fear & Greed Index
indicator.description: A daily composite index designed by CNN to measure prevailing fear and greed in the U.S. stock market using multiple market-behavior indicators. The index ranges from 0 to 100, with lower values representing greater fear and higher values representing greater greed.
indicator.use: Monitor changes in U.S. equity-market sentiment, investor risk appetite, market momentum, volatility, and demand for defensive assets, and identify shifts between risk-seeking and risk-averse market conditions.
indicator.purpose: Provide a compact market-sentiment signal that summarizes several observable characteristics of U.S. equity markets into a single daily measure for tracking changes in investor risk appetite and market stress.
indicator.significance: The Fear & Greed Index provides a behavioral measure of the prevailing emotional conditions in U.S. equity markets. Changes in the index can indicate shifts in market momentum, volatility, demand for safe-haven assets, and willingness to take risk. It can therefore provide context for interpreting market moves alongside prices, volatility measures, credit conditions, and broader financial-market indicators.

results.title: Dollar Gains Amid Hawkish Fed Commentary and Rising Geopolitical Tensions | Investing.com
highlights: * Fed’s Hammack sounds hawkish, Middle-East tensions escalate * Oil prices revive inflation fears, but Fed bets steady ahead of US CPI data * RBA leaves door open to additional hikes, BoJ expected to hike gradually * Wall Street trades cautiously as major US banks kick off earnings season The US dollar strengthened against all its major peers on Monday, driven by hawkish Fed commentary and renewed tensions in the Middle East. Today, the greenback is pulling back, perhaps as traders are adjusting their positions ahead of the resumption of Treasury trading today and the US CPI data tomorrow. Cleveland Fed President Beth Hammack sounded hawkish yesterday, warning that inflation expectations could become less anchored if policymakers delay in taking action and suggesting that the neutral rate may be higher than previously estimated. Her comments came as oil prices rebounded amid new tensions and strikes in the Middle East and Ukraine. With the reopening of the Strait of Hormuz becoming a far-fetched dream once again and Russia carrying out strikes on Ukraine, including damage to a thermal power plant in Kharkiv, thereby violating the proposed energy ceasefire, oil prices rebounded, intensifying inflation fears once again. Having said all that though, investors’ expectations about the future course of the Fed’s actions have not been impacted. Market participants still assign a 20% chance of an October hike, fully pricing in move for December. By the end of 2027, a total of 80bps worth of hikes is baked into the cake. Today, two more Fed officials will step onto the rostrum: Richmond Fed President Thomas Barkin and Boston Fed President Susan Collins. It will be interesting to see whether they share Hamack’s hawkish views or lean towards those of Vice Fed Chair Jefferson and New York Fed President Williams, who have suggested that the Committee should not rush into pressing the hike button too soon. As for tomorrow’s CPI inflation data, both the S&P Global and ISM price-related subindices suggest that the risks may be tilted to the upside. Therefore, hotter-than-expected prints could add more fuel to the dollar’s engines, even if they don’t significantly boost the chances of an October hike. They could add more basis points worth of rate hikes for next year. Elsewhere, the minutes of the latest RBA meeting revealed that policymakers believed the upside inflation risks identified earlier had already materialized or started building, leaving the door open to another rate increase if inflation proves more persistent than expected. The probability of another rate hike before the turn of the year continues to hover near 50%. A strong employment report on Thursday could take that probability higher. The International Monetary Fund (IMF) said today that the Bank of Japan (BoJ) will likely raise interest rates gradually toward a neutral setting, despite an expected slowdown in growth. The yen is gaining some ground against the dollar today, but the overall picture remains negative. A couple of weeks ago, investors were pricing in 100bps worth of additional rate hikes by the end of 2027. Now the number has dropped to 90bps. With Prime Minister Takaichi insisting on fiscal spending and calling for the BoJ to keep interest rates low, it may be hard to envision a more hawkish Bank than currently expected. After all, Takaichi has already appointed two doves when she had the opportunity – those members dissented the latest hike – and she could appoint two more next summer, when the term of two ultra-hawks ends. On Wall Street, both the S&P 500 and the Nasdaq closed slightly in the red on Monday, with only the Dow Jones adding some gains. Perhaps the reason why there was no material decline following Hammack’s remarks was the anticipated start of the bank earnings season later today. What’s more, trading was less informative because the US Treasury market was closed for Columbus Day. JPMorgan (NYSE: JPM), Goldman Sachs (NYSE: GS), Citigroup (NYSE: C) and Wells Fargo are all due to report today, followed by Bank of America and Morgan Stanley on Wednesday. The key question for bank earnings may be how severely tightening financial conditions amid rising yields have weighed on credit demand.

results.title: Big Bank Earnings Meet a Key CPI Report: What to Watch This Week as the S&P 500 Hovers Near Records - Liberty Markets.us
highlights: JPMorgan, Goldman Sachs, Citigroup and Wells Fargo report today, and September CPI lands Wednesday, with the 10-year yield near 5.2% and the Fed meeting two weeks out. Here is what the data and strategists say to watch. Matt Hardy October 13, 2026 7 minutes read This is the first big test of third-quarter earnings season and of the inflation data that will shape the Fed’s next move. JPMorgan Chase, Goldman Sachs, Citigroup and Wells Fargo report before the open today (Tuesday, October 13), with Morgan Stanley and Bank of America due Wednesday, according to a Reuters week-ahead preview. The September CPI report is also due Wednesday, October 14. Reuters’ poll expects headline CPI of 3.6% year over year and core CPI of 2.5%, while the 10-year Treasury yield sits around 5.23%, near its highest level in 24 years. The Fed meets October 27-28, after raising rates in September for the first time since 2023. Results were not yet known at the time of writing, so this article focuses on what to watch rather than what happened. Per Reuters, the S&P 500 hit an all-time closing high last Tuesday, its first since mid-August, and is up more than 13% year to date despite declines on Wednesday and Thursday. Reuters also notes that LSEG IBES expects third-quarter S&P 500 earnings to grow more than 30%, following a strong first half. Our own coverage of the prior quarter is in S&P 500 Q2 2026 Earnings: Strongest Growth Since 2021, which provides useful context for how high the earnings bar has become. The weak spot is financials. Reuters reports the S&P 500 banks index fell about 9% over the past month, among the market’s weakest groups as Treasury yields rose. That sets up an unusual dynamic: the sector reporting first is also the one carrying the most skepticism. Matthew Miskin, co-chief investment strategist at Manulife John Hancock Investments, told Reuters: “Earnings have been incredible this year, and we’re just going to have to start to see with the banks how Q3 shaped up.” He added that he expects “a sigh of relief if these financial services companies come out with good results next week.” Beyond headline EPS the following items - Net interest income guidance: Higher rates can widen lending margins, but they can also raise funding costs. - Credit quality: Loan-loss provisions and card delinquencies show how consumers and businesses are coping with higher borrowing costs. - Capital markets activity: Trading and investment banking revenue is a major swing factor for Goldman Sachs and Morgan Stanley. - Management tone: Commentary on the consumer and the economy often moves shares as much as the numbers. The September CPI report arrives Wednesday, October 14. The Reuters poll points to 3.6% annual headline inflation and 2.5% core, against the Fed’s 2% target. A separate consensus compiled by MarketWatch and cited by Stocktwits is slightly different, at +0.6% month over month and 3.7% year over year for headline, and +0.2% month over month and 2.5% year over year for core. The gap between forecasts is small, but it is a reminder that “consensus” is not one number. The headline-versus-core gap is the story. A headline reading well above core points to energy as a major driver, which fits the oil-driven volatility we have covered in Stocks Rebound Sharply the Day After the Fed’s Rate Hike. Reuters adds that producer price and retail sales reports are also due this week. According to Reuters, traders have reduced bets on another rate hike at the October 27-28 meeting, but hotter data could revive them. Matt Stucky, chief portfolio manager for equities at Northwestern Mutual Wealth Management, said: “If you start to see more evidence of re-accelerating inflation that’s not going to come down absent a full hiking cycle from the Fed, that’s where equity markets really can be under pressure.” Michael Reynolds of Glenmede put the focus on services: “We really want to see material progress on (core services inflation) to get a little bit more confident that the Fed doesn’t have to be as aggressive as maybe the market’s pricing in,” adding that “at some point, major indices are going to cry uncle on higher rates.” Stocktwits also notes that Kevin Warsh is scheduled to speak Thursday at the IMF and World Bank annual meetings, and that Cleveland Fed President Beth Hammack has a speaking engagement the same day. Reuters says the 10-year yield was around 5.23% late last week. Many investors had treated 5% as a key threshold for stock market pressure, yet the market has so far absorbed yields above that level. We examined the rate backdrop in Stocks Slide as 10-Year Treasury Yield Hits Highest Level Since 2007. A hot CPI print could test how durable that tolerance is, while a benign one could ease pressure on rate-sensitive sectors, including banks. - Solid bank results and cooler CPI: Could support the “sigh of relief” Miskin describes and ease yield pressure. - Solid bank results but hot CPI: Strong earnings may be overshadowed by renewed rate-hike fears. - Weak bank guidance and hot CPI: The most challenging combination for a market near record highs. Per Reuters, JPMorgan, Goldman Sachs, Citigroup and Wells Fargo report Tuesday, October 13, and Morgan Stanley and Bank of America report Wednesday. BlackRock is also expected this week. Reuters says it is due Wednesday, October 14. The Reuters poll expects 3.6% headline and 2.5% core inflation year over year. The Fed raised rates in September and meets again October 27-28. Hotter inflation data could revive bets on another hike, which strategists quoted by Reuters flag as a risk for equities. Reuters reports the S&P 500 banks index fell about 9% over the past month amid rising Treasury yields. The article does not attribute the decline to a single cause.

results.title: STIR: Fed Pricing Unmoved By Weekly ADP; Hike Pri- 10-13-2026 | MNI
highlights: STIR: Fed Pricing Unmoved By Weekly ADP; Hike Pri- 10-13-2026 | MNI STIR: Fed Pricing Unmoved By Weekly ADP; Hike Priced Through Dec The US$ front end once again looks through lower tier labor market data (weekly ADP employment print - Persistently above-target inflation readings will lead the FOMC to hike rates for the first time since 2023 at its September meeting, with the Fed funds rate range rising 25bp to 3.75-4.00%. - While there may be a dissent or two in favor of a hold, overall we think Chair Warsh will lead the Committee to take action given evidence that disinflation has stalled, recalling his Jackson Hole declaration that “we must be confident that underlying inflation is moving to our objective, clearly and at sufficient speed. Otherwise, we have work to do.” - We don’t think the outcome will be altogether hawkish however. The 25bp hike is largely priced and there doesn’t appear to be significant appetite at this stage for a major hiking cycle, even among Committee hawks. - As such we think the Dot Plot will reflect a core Committee view that two or at most three hikes will be sufficient to return policy to a restrictive enough stance to get inflation converging to target at a reasonable pace before cuts can resume by 2028. - That’s more dovish than current market pricing which shows both an 80% implied probability of a 25bp hike at this meeting and a follow-up priced by December, with just under 100bp tightening total to the peak over the coming year. - Warsh is once again very unlikely to offer forward guidance on future meetings. Even if as is likely he downplays the signal from the Dot Plot’s indication of just one more hike this year, his inflation-fighting rhetoric is unlikely to go any further than his Jackson Hole speech, limiting the scope for surprising hawkish takeaways from the meeting. US INFLATION: MNI US Inflation Insight: Firm Core Prices Seal Deal For Hike - While August’s inflation data didn’t show a major acceleration in underlying pressures, nor will they have offered comfort to Fed participants who are looking for more decisive indications of progress toward the 2% target. - Core CPI rose 0.29% M/M, above the 0.22% consensus and July’s 0.22%. The upside surprise was driven by supercore inflation, with core goods coming in on the soft side of expectations. - Headline CPI was broadly in line with consensus. The monthly acceleration reflected a rebound in energy prices, while food inflation remained relatively tame. Grocery prices were flat, but food away from home remained on the warm side and indicative of continued service-sector price pressures. - The main upside drivers in core were arguably outliers: a record increase in wireless telephone services, a rebound in lodging, and less-negative car insurance. Housing was softer than expected, while medical services were relatively benign. - However, inflation remained broad and elevated by pre-pandemic standards, and supercore trends picked up from softer prior readings. - The PPI report showed more moderate pipeline pressures compared to July, but run rates remained elevated amid continued energy passthrough. PCE-relevant components—including airfares and parts of healthcare -- looked on the firm side. - As a result, core PCE tracking moved into the 0.25–0.30% M/M area (vs 0.21-0.22% coming into the inflation round), with consensus clustered in the high 0.20s. That would translate roughly into a 2.7-2.8% core PCE run rate on a 3-month annualized basis, with Y/Y continuing to run well above 3%. - Gov Warsh and most of the FOMC are unlikely to be convinced that this represents anything close to a resumption of disinflationary progress. Accordingly, the data were enough to see market-implied pricing for a September Fed hike firm to well over 80%, from under 60% prior to PPI. Analyst estimates for August core PCE picked up again after Friday's CPI data. Prior to the release, an early median of analysts had seen core PCE at 0.24-0.25% M/M, similar to 0.25% in July; it had been around 0.21-0.22% pre-PPI; consensus now appears to be clustered in the high 0.20s. pre-CPI

results.title: BlackRock cuts US stocks to neutral and buys Treasuries as 10-year yield nears 5.25%
highlights: BlackRock cuts US stocks to neutral and buys Treasuries as 10-year yield nears 5.25% * BlackRock cut US equities to neutral from overweight in a short-term risk-management move and upgraded short-dated Treasuries to overweight, saying markets have overpriced 160bp of Fed tightening as 10-year yields climbed to around 5.25% this year. BlackRock’s shift adds weight to the case that higher yields are starting to compete with equities for capital, a dynamic that could cap stock valuations even as earnings stay strong. The key swing factor is oil: Middle East war and higher crude prices have driven the sharp repricing of Fed expectations, so any easing in the Iran war would support BlackRock’s view that rate-hike bets are overdone and favour its short-end Treasury call. Conversely, a further oil spike that lifts this week’s CPI and PPI could push yields higher still and test the cushion BlackRock estimates before Treasury returns turn negative. Demand from large allocators at these yields may also help steady the long end after recent volatility, while the trimmed JGB underweight suggests Japanese yields above 3% are drawing more interest. * BlackRock closed its long-held overweight on US equities, moving to neutral, describing it as a short-term risk-management step in a volatile macro and market environment * The firm said its core convictions on AI transformation remain intact, and it still favours AI-related companies, listed infrastructure and emerging market equities * It upgraded shorter-term Treasuries to overweight and long-term Treasuries to neutral, ending an underweight held for most of the past six years * BlackRock said the 160 basis points of additional Fed tightening priced in since January is overdone, with the 10-year yield up 110 basis points this year to around 5.25% * It estimates a cushion of about 75 basis points against further yield rises over 12 months before Treasury total returns turn negative * The firm also trimmed its underweight on Japanese government bonds and cut US agency mortgage-backed securities to neutral to help fund the shift BlackRock has closed its long-held overweight position in US equities, moving to neutral as part of a shift that sees the world’s largest asset manager adding US Treasuries after rising yields made government bonds more attractive. The firm described the equity downgrade as a short-term risk-management move rather than a change in its core views, saying investors need to be more dynamic in today’s volatile macro and market regime. It said it is also watching growing public attention to AI policy and to the build-out of AI infrastructure across US jurisdictions. BlackRock said its convictions on AI transformation remain intact. It argued that higher rates are increasingly separating companies that can generate returns above their cost of capital from those that cannot, and it continues to favour AI-related companies and listed infrastructure, where strong demand and scarcity support returns. It also kept its overweight on emerging market equities. The move comes even as third-quarter earnings for S&P 500 companies are expected to grow nearly 30% from a year earlier, according to FactSet data cited in the note. Proceeds from taking profits on US stocks are partly funding a significant upgrade to Treasuries. BlackRock said the 10-year Treasury yield has risen 110 basis points this year to around 5.25%, driven mainly by higher real interest rates rather than inflation expectations or term premium, the extra return investors demand for holding longer-dated bonds. It attributed the rise in real rates to intensifying competition for capital, which is pushing up the neutral rate, and to a sharp reversal in Fed expectations driven by Middle East tensions and higher oil prices. Markets have priced in 160 basis points of additional Fed tightening over the next 12 months since January, which BlackRock considers overdone. The firm upgraded shorter-term Treasuries to overweight, where it sees the most scope for tightening expectations to unwind, and long-term Treasuries to neutral, saying higher yields now better compensate investors for interest rate risk. BlackRock said it had been underweight Treasuries for most of the past six years, first moving there in October 2020 when 10-year yields were near 0.9%. At current levels, it estimates yields could rise a further 75 basis points over 12 months before total returns turn negative. In other changes, BlackRock trimmed its underweight on Japanese government bonds, a position held since July 2023 when 10-year yields were around 0.4% to 0.5%, compared with above 3% now. It also cut US agency mortgage-backed securities to neutral. The firm said it stands ready to add risk again as visibility improves. This week’s US CPI and PPI reports, the first snapshots of September inflation, are likely to shape Fed rate expectations and Treasury yields. **Why its calls matter:** when a manager this size shifts its views, as it did today by cutting US stocks to neutral and adding Treasuries, the change can steer flows across its model portfolios and is closely watched by other investors as a signal of institutional sentiment.

She said current policy is not restrictive enough, that the neutral rate 'may be higher, but is hard to determine', and that rate hikes are unlikely to address the key inflation drivers — tariffs and AI-related demand. Yet the long end is already doing the work: Freddie Mac's 30-year fixed mortgage hit 7.4% on Oct 8, Redfin's pending home sales fell 4% m/m in September to the lowest since 2014, and US Treasury yields sit at multi-decade highs. The Fed enters pre-meeting blackout Saturday ahead of the Oct 28 decision, with Wednesday's September CPI as the decisive print. Hammack's Monday NABE speech hardened the hawkish flank heading into the Fed's pre-meeting blackout (begins Saturday; meeting ends Oct 28) [1] [2]. She did not call for an October move, but made the case that policy is not yet restrictive enough and should arrive in smaller, more frequent increments rather than after a backlog builds [1] [3]. The long end is already pricing that message: 30-year mortgage at 7.4%, pending home sales at a 12-year low, Treasury yields at multi-decade highs [4] [5]. Wednesday's September CPI decides whether October stays on hold or whether Hammack's 'smaller, faster' framing gets traction [2]. - **[ESCALATED] Hawkish — Beth Hammack (Cleveland Fed, 2026 voter):** at NABE in Cleveland Monday, said she generally prefers 'smaller adjustmentsrelatively quickly' over waiting for a larger course correction [1] [3]. Stopped short of backing a hike this month [3]. Said current policy's restrictiveness is insufficient [6], that the neutral rate 'may be higher, but is hard to determine' [7], and that her own neutral-rate estimate sits 'on the high end' of FOMC participants (single-source relay) [8]. results.title: Fed's Waller: Surging Treasury Yields Reflect Growth and AI Investment, Not Inflation
highlights: Fed's Waller: Surging Treasury Yields Reflect Growth and AI Investment, Not Inflation - Fed Governor Christopher Waller said rising long-term Treasury yields are driven by strong economic growth and AI-related investment, not inflation expectations. - He warned that weaker safe-haven demand for U.S. debt could be adding 50–70 basis points to yields, though that figure is attributed to Waller and not independently verified. - Waller expects the AI investment boom to continue for another 2–3 years, but he still sees inflation as too high and further rate hikes may be needed if data warrant. Rising U.S. Treasury yields are not a warning sign of unanchored inflation expectations, according to Federal Reserve Governor Christopher Waller. Instead, they reflect a powerful combination of robust economic growth and an artificial intelligence investment boom that is soaking up capital, he said Tuesday at Bloomberg’s New Economy Forum in New Delhi. Speaking to an audience of global financiers, Waller argued that the surge in long-term borrowing costs—which has pushed 10-year Treasury yields to multi-year highs—is largely a function of stronger growth prospects and increased competition for funding from AI infrastructure projects. He also pointed to a diminished safe-haven premium for U.S. government debt, which he estimated could be adding 50 to 70 basis points to yields. That estimate, attributed to Waller, has not been independently confirmed by market data. Waller’s remarks come at a delicate moment for monetary policy. The Fed raised its benchmark rate by 25 basis points in September to a range of 3.75%–4.00%, ending a nine-month pause. In an October 8 speech, Waller said inflation remained “too high” and that additional increases would likely be needed if incoming data followed his expectations. The latest reading of core personal consumption expenditures inflation showed a 3% annual rate—well above the Fed’s 2% target. Yet Waller’s tone on Tuesday suggested that higher long-term yields are already doing some of the Fed’s work. He specifically noted that interest-sensitive sectors like housing and automobiles are cooling, which could reduce the need for further policy tightening. The distinction is important: Waller is not signaling a pause, but he is acknowledging that market forces are providing some restraint. Waller’s argument that AI investment is driving yields higher rests on a simple premise: massive capital expenditures for data centers, semiconductors, and energy infrastructure are competing for a limited pool of savings, pushing real interest rates up. That dynamic, in turn, supports higher Treasury yields even if inflation expectations remain anchored. But the Fed governor also acknowledged that the AI boom is contributing to inflation in specific corners of the economy. In his October speech, he flagged that AI-driven demand for high-tech components—such as advanced chips and servers—has pushed up prices for those goods. He also cited elevated energy costs and potential new tariffs as obstacles to disinflation. The tension is clear: AI spending supports growth, but it also raises financing costs for the very investments that are fueling that growth. Reuters (TRI) reported in September that persistent inflation and further Fed tightening could materially affect AI capital expenditure plans. So far, however, there is little evidence of a slowdown. Waller said he expects the AI investment cycle to continue for another two to three years—a forecast that, like his yield estimate, is attributed to him and not independently verified. Waller’s comments also touched on the fiscal outlook. He has previously argued that structural deficits—currently around 6% of GDP—would need to move much closer to zero for the U.S. to grow its way out of its debt burden. He has expressed skepticism that short-term Treasury buybacks would meaningfully lower borrowing costs. The global appeal of U.S. debt is another factor. The erosion of the safe-haven premium, which Waller attributed to research by Stanford’s Hanno Lustig, means investors are demanding a higher return for holding Treasuries even as a reserve asset. That could complicate the dollar’s role in global markets, though Waller did not suggest the dollar’s status is at risk. He also noted that geopolitical tensions in the Middle East and ongoing trade disputes could keep energy prices volatile and add to tariff-related price pressures. Markets will be watching incoming inflation and employment data to see if Waller’s growth-led explanation holds. The next Fed meeting is scheduled for December, and while no change is expected, the central bank’s statement and updated projections will be scrutinized for any shift in the reaction function. For now, Waller’s message is clear: the bond market is not flashing an inflation warning; it is responding to a world of stronger growth, massive AI investment, and a diminished safety premium. Whether that narrative survives the next round of data is an open question.

For the past fortnight, coverage from CNBC to FXStreet has framed the slide largely as a French debt story, 3,4 and KBC summed it up in six words: “Euro weakness took over from dollar strength”. 4 Yet by Monday, Société Générale described the French-German bond spread as stagnating, while hawkish Fed commentary, firmer oil, and fresh geopolitical headlines lined up with the dollar’s gains. 1,2 EUR/USD fell to near 1.1150 on 12 October 2026, its weakest level since May 2025, as hawkish Fed comments and firmer oil lifted the dollar. KBC data showed the French 10-year government bond (OAT) swap spread widening from 80bp at the end of August to an all-time high above 140bp in the week to 2 October, as investors weighed a draft budget implying at least another year with a deficit of around 5%. 4 In plain terms, investors demanded a bigger premium to hold French debt, and the euro footed part of the bill. KBC’s swap-spread figure is a different measure from the French-German bond spread Société Générale cites below, so the two numbers are not directly comparable. The ECB raised its deposit rate to 2.50% on 10 September, 6 yet KBC noted that money markets scaled back ECB tightening bets as spreads widened, even after flash euro-area inflation came in at 3.8% year on year in September. 4 By 29 September the pair had touched 1.1312, and Bloomberg reported the euro was on course for its worst month since July 2025. 8 Monday’s fresh low arrived without a fresh leg of French stress. Société Générale described the 10-year OAT/Bund spread as stagnating around 137bp, which, in the bank’s view, removed one source of euro weakness. 2 French fiscal worries had not gone away, and FXStreet also flagged Spain’s snap general election on 29 November, 2 but the spread itself was not widening. Cleveland Fed President Beth Hammack argued for higher interest rates as inflation broadens, and West Texas Intermediate (WTI) crude finished Monday up more than 1.60% at $93.17 as tensions around the Strait of Hormuz and doubts over a Russia-Ukraine ceasefire on energy facilities kept supply worries alive. 1 EUR/USD traded near 1.1155, down 0.40%, late in the New York session. 1 For more on the policy side, see our Federal Reserve news feed. Our US dollar news coverage tracks how that pricing shifts. Put together, Monday’s 17-month low looks less like a new euro problem and more like the dollar picking up where French bonds left off. Monday’s 17-month low came with French spreads flat and US cash bonds closed; the dollar side of EUR/USD appeared to do the work. Ebury’s base case is that the Fed holds in October; its Global Head of Market Strategy, Matthew Ryan, expects “a moderate (i.e. 0.2% or less) monthly core print” on Wednesday and noted that an upside surprise could quickly revive pricing for an October Fed hike. 7 On the euro side, Citi analysts flagged that French fiscal risk could lead the ECB to pause its hikes after December, or sooner if stress spreads. 2 Any euro US dollar forecast built this week rests on those two variables. - US CPI, 14 October: September CPI data is due at 08:30 ET, or 20:30 (GMT+8), which parks the week’s main US release in the Asian dinner hour. 2 - US Producer Prices and Retail Sales, 15 October: Producer Price Index (PPI) and retail sales data follow on Thursday. 2 - Fed Chair Kevin Warsh, This Week: FXStreet listed Warsh among the Fed speakers due this week, after Hammack’s Monday remarks. 1 - French Spreads, Daily: Société Générale placed the 10-year OAT/Bund spread near 137bp against a longer-run mean of about 110bp; 2 renewed widening would put the euro side back in focus. - Fed and ECB Decisions, 28 and 29 October: The FOMC announces its October decision on 28 October, and the ECB Governing Council follows on 29 October. 3,9 Monday’s low looked like a holiday fluke at first: a 17-month extreme printed while US cash bonds were closed. The evidence points somewhere plainer. The euro side, French spreads, was steady; the dollar side, Fed rhetoric and oil, was not. 1,2 Wednesday’s CPI tests that dollar side directly, and the French spread remains the variable that could bring the euro side back to the front.

highlights: The US Dollar Index held near a yearly high of 102.61 on 13 October as Treasury yields eased to around 5.20%. ING analysts say markets are focused on US growth, elevated inflation and the prospect of 75 basis points in further rate hikes. Although US bond markets were closed for a holiday, the US Dollar Index showed remarkable resilience during the 12 October 2026 trading session, holding firmly at elevated levels and extending its strength in the following day's European session. Behind this lies robust US economic data, persistent inflationary pressure, and deep market expectations regarding the Federal Reserve's policy path. During the European session on 13 October, the US Dollar Index, which measures the greenback against six major currencies, edged down 0.17% to trade near 102.38, just a step away from the fresh yearly high of 102.61 set on 12 October, with bulls still in control of the market. US bond markets were closed on 12 October for the long holiday weekend; after reopening on 13 October, the ten-year Treasury yield fell back 0.85% to around 5.20%, though this brief pullback did little to undermine the dollar's overall tone of strength. Market experts broadly agree that the outlook for the dollar remains positive, underpinned by the US economy's solid growth, persistently elevated inflation, and firm expectations that the Federal Reserve will adopt a more aggressive policy path. Analysts at ING noted that the foreign exchange market is currently filtering out recent short-term noise and refocusing on the key cyclical narratives: - Solid US economic growth; - Inflation running above target; - The broad prospect of the Federal Reserve raising rates by a further 75 basis points from current levels. Upcoming macroeconomic data will serve as a litmus test for market sentiment. Investors are closely watching the US September CPI and PPI figures, due for release on the evenings of 14 and 15 October, which are expected to have a profound impact on future interest rate expectations. Several regional Fed presidents have also issued clear guidance, noting that inflationary concerns remain elevated and that further rate hikes will be necessary to keep price pressures under control. Among the many statements from regional Fed presidents, remarks by Hammack stood out for their strikingly hawkish stance and drew widespread market attention. According to data from the FXS Speechtracker, Hammack's speech scored 8.4, well above the historical average of 7.5, clearly indicating that her push for policy tightening goes far beyond the conventional baseline. Hammack stated that, in order to force inflation down to the 2% policy target, the Federal Reserve must maintain a restrictive policy stance and keep benchmark interest rates at higher levels. Hammack further noted that, against a backdrop of broadly neutral financial conditions, demand-driven price pressures are spreading widely, even extending to emerging sectors such as artificial intelligence. She expressed concern that an inflationary mindset is gradually becoming entrenched, and warned that some companies are planning to raise end-product prices further beyond basic input costs, which undoubtedly heightens the risk of inflation becoming anchored. She stressed that the Federal Reserve should adopt a strategy of swift, incremental rate adjustments to act pre-emptively, preventing inflation expectations from spiralling further out of control and stopping inflation from becoming an intractable problem. The shortfall hit AI stocks and lifted bonds. The S&P 500 remains pinned below its mid-August highs, while weakness outside tech in July hinted at growth sensitivity masked by AI enthusiasm.
