Three variables deserve your attention: * Core CPI month-on-month against **0.2%** * Retail sales after stripping out the oil distortion * How fast breakevens and Treasuries move after each print Conflicting headline forecasts and an unconfirmed **50 bp** gap are reasons to think in scenarios rather than certainties. Your view should shift on a core surprise or a spending miss, not on a gasoline-driven headline. The probability of an October hike fell from 64.2% on 25 September to 22.1% on 9 October, and expected tightening by December shrank from about 36 bp to 26 bp. The 2027 hike pricing, roughly 50 bp above the Fed's path per the original source, is the part of the curve most exposed to a soft print.

results.title: Bond Market Backs Off 24-Year High as September CPI Looms
highlights: Bond Market Backs Off 24-Year High as September CPI Looms U.S. Treasury yields backed away from their highest levels in nearly a quarter-century on Tuesday as a drop in oil prices and fading risk appetite gave bond investors a temporary reprieve — but the real test arrives Wednesday, when the Bureau of Labor Statistics releases September consumer price inflation data at 8:30 a.m. ET. The bond market is pre-positioning for the print. Prediction markets are not quite ready to call a ceasefire on the December rate hike trade. The 10-year Treasury yield, the benchmark for mortgages, corporate debt, and the primary driver of rate-hike expectations, fell 5.5 basis points to 5.189% in European trading Tuesday. That puts it 17.6 basis points below the 24-year high of 5.365% struck last week. The 30-year yield declined 4 basis points to 5.5524%, and the 2-year note — the instrument most sensitive to Fed policy — fell more than 2 basis points to 4.7679%. Two catalysts drove Tuesday's bond rally. First, oil prices fell sharply after investors assessed the implications of the U.S.-brokered "energy ceasefire" between Russia and Ukraine, which has raised the prospect of more Russian diesel entering global markets. Because elevated energy prices — driven largely by the ongoing Iran war and disruptions to the Strait of Hormuz — have been a primary engine of inflation this year, any cooling in crude exerts downstream pressure on bond yields. Second, a pullback in AI-related stocks reduced the risk-on appetite that had been compressing demand for safe-haven government bonds. "This combination of easing risk appetite and fading inflation concerns from the commodity side of the equation has created a fillip for government bonds," said Simon Ballard, chief economist at First Abu Dhabi Bank. Treasury markets also reopened Tuesday after closing Monday for the Columbus Day holiday, adding some technical momentum to the move. Consensus forecasts put September's headline CPI at 3.6% to 3.7% year-over-year, up from August's 3.4% annual rate. The acceleration is almost entirely energy-driven — analysts project the energy component to rise roughly 5.5% on a month-over-month basis, the largest monthly contribution since March, reflecting higher pump prices tied to Middle East supply disruptions. On a monthly basis, headline CPI is expected to rise 0.5% to 0.6% — an ugly number that the market is already discounting. The number that actually moves markets is the core reading. Core CPI — which strips out volatile food and energy prices and is the Fed's preferred inflation signal — is expected to rise just 0.2% month-over-month, a slowdown from August's 0.3% print. That would hold the annual core rate steady at approximately 2.4% to 2.5%. Analysts note that August's 5.4% spike in telephone services costs, which distorted the prior core reading higher, is widely expected to reverse and not recur. Citi's economics team projects an even softer 0.18% monthly core print. The Federal Reserve meets October 27-28, and the October hike probability is priced at roughly 19% on CME FedWatch — a figure low enough that even a modest upside surprise is unlikely to meaningfully change the October calculus. "We do not believe that the report will sway the Fed into hiking later this month," said Thierry Wizman, global FX and rates strategist at Macquarie Group. Citi added that even a 0.3% monthly core reading would be "insufficient to justify a rate hike in October." The October meeting may be effectively settled, but December is not. Polymarket traders priced a 75.5% chance of a 25-basis-point Fed rate hike at the December meeting as of late Sunday, with $3.0 million in volume traded on that contract. The October hike market tells the same story from the other direction: 80.5% of the $33.6 million traded on the October no-hike contract bets the Fed stands pat later this month. Kalshi traders, meanwhile, put less than one-in-three odds on inflation hitting a new 2026 high, and expect September CPI to print at approximately 3.6% year-over-year — consistent with consensus and a view that the energy shock is peaking rather than accelerating. The prediction market setup is a classic skip-and-hike structure: October is off the table, December remains live. That positioning aligns with the Fed's own signals — minutes from the September FOMC meeting showed officials did not make an urgent case for an immediate follow-on hike, with several suggesting any further move could wait until December. Three total hikes over the next 12 months remain fully priced in futures-derived estimates, meaning the debate is not whether rates will rise further, but when. The core CPI print Wednesday will be the most consequential data point in that debate. A 0.2% monthly core reading — or softer — would reinforce the skip narrative, relieve pressure on 2-year yields, and likely compress the spread between October hike odds and December hike odds. A surprise at 0.3% or above would be more disruptive, potentially pushing the term premium higher and raising questions about whether December could become a November conversation. BlackRock made one of the week's most notable macro positioning moves, cutting U.S. equities to neutral from overweight and upgrading short-dated Treasuries to overweight. The firm argued that the 160 basis points of additional Fed tightening priced into markets since January is "overdone," and that the 10-year yield's 110-basis-point rise this year to approximately 5.25% has created genuine value for bond buyers at the front end. Goldman Sachs has recommended positioning in interest-rate swaps to benefit from a relative rally in the 10-year versus the 5-year and 30-year. Morgan Stanley said current yields already offer investment value unless nominal GDP compounds above 5.7% over the next decade — a scenario few serious forecasters endorse. The bond market's Tuesday move is not a verdict on inflation — it is a pre-CPI positioning shift by investors who believe the core print comes in soft and the oil-driven headline acceleration does not change October's calculus. For December-hike traders on Kalshi and Polymarket, Wednesday morning is the event. If core CPI prints at 0.2% or below and yields continue their retreat from the 24-year high, expect December hike odds to face real compression. If the print surprises to the upside, 75.5% looks like a floor, not a ceiling.

results.title: Why Stocks and Bonds are RALLYING After Fed Rate Hike! (Market Update) (2026)
highlights: If you had asked me yesterday what the market reaction to a Federal Reserve interest rate hike would be, I probably would have predicted a bloodbath. Logic suggests that when the cost of borrowing goes up, equity valuations go down. Yet, Thursday morning saw a completely different reality: stocks soared, bonds rallied, and investors seemed to be throwing a party. It is a classic example of how market psychology often defies basic economic textbook rules, and personally, I find this disconnect absolutely fascinating. What we witnessed wasn't just a reaction to numbers on a screen; it was a massive vote of confidence in a new era of central banking leadership. The market isn't reacting to the rate hike itself, but rather to the person wielding the hammer. One thing that immediately stands out to me is the sheer impact of Kevin Warsh’s communication style. After a period of confusion where bond yields spiked to multi-decade highs, leaving investors grasping at straws, Warsh stepped into the spotlight and provided something the markets crave more than anything else: clarity. By delivering a press conference that was described as "coherent" and "consistently hawkish," he effectively ended the guessing game. From my perspective, this is the most critical takeaway from the day. What many people don't realize is that markets can actually price in uncertainty much more easily than they can price in a known, albeit painful, reality. When the Fed is indecisive, volatility explodes. By being "hawkish without being crazy," as one analyst put it, Warsh has managed to "thread the needle." Personally, I think this suggests we are entering a phase where the Fed's greatest asset isn't its ability to move rates, but its ability to manage expectations. This is a huge shift from the era of "transparency" that often felt more like "constant surprises." Furthermore, the fact that the Fed chose to defy the political pressure from the Trump administration to hike rates is a detail I find especially interesting. It signals that the institution is fighting to preserve its independence. If the Fed loses its reputation as an autonomous body, the long-term implications for global bond markets would be catastrophic. This move wasn't just about inflation; it was about institutional survival. While the Fed provided the psychological floor, the cooling of oil prices provided the actual fuel for the rally. Seeing U.S. crude dip below the $100 mark is a significant psychological milestone. What makes this particularly fascinating is the cocktail of geopolitical factors driving this decline. We are seeing a convergence of potential diplomacy—specifically the rumors of President Trump discussing the Iran situation with Gulf leaders—and the physical reality of Saudi Arabia potentially restoring its pipeline capacity. If you take a step back and think about it, the market is essentially betting on a de-escalation of the "geopolitical risk premium." For months, oil has been trading at a premium not just because of supply and demand, but because of the fear of sudden, violent disruptions. When that fear recedes, even slightly, it acts like a massive shot of adrenaline for the S&P 500 and the Nasdaq. However, I must offer a word of caution: despite this dip, oil prices are still up over 65% since the start of the year. This rally feels like a relief valve being opened, not a permanent end to the era of high energy costs. Despite the green numbers on the tickers, I can't help but feel a sense of underlying fragility in this rally. This raises a deeper question: is this a genuine recovery, or just a momentary sigh of relief before the next wave of pain? - The "Higher for Longer" Reality: Fed officials have already signaled that more hikes are likely before the year ends. We aren't at the peak; we are likely just climbing the mountain. - The Diesel Disconnect: While crude is dipping, retail diesel prices have surged nearly 93% in a month. This is a massive drag on the real economy that won't show up in a stock index rally until it's too late. - Global Contagion: The Bank of Japan is expected to move on interest rates very soon. In our hyper-connected global economy, a move in Tokyo can trigger a massive liquidation in New York. What this really suggests is that the market is currently in a state of "hopeful denial." It is celebrating the clarity of the Fed and the dip in oil, while simultaneously ignoring the fact that the fundamental cost of doing business is still rising. In my opinion, we are seeing a market that is highly sensitive to sentiment but remains dangerously exposed to the structural reality of inflation. Ultimately, Thursday was a masterclass in how markets interpret leadership. The rally wasn't an endorsement of high interest rates; it was an endorsement of a predictable central bank. But we must be careful not to mistake predictability for stability. The Fed is walking a tightrope, and while Kevin Warsh may have found his footing, the economic landscape beneath him remains incredibly volatile. Personally, I think investors should enjoy this rally, but they should do so with one eye firmly on the exit sign.

results.title: Weekly Global Economic Update | Deloitte Insights
highlights: * Fiscal policy is driving bond yields higher in some developed economies * US inflation eases * Whither US consumers? * In the United States, government borrowing costs have increased sharply, with the yield on the 30-year bond hitting its highest level in two decades. This suggests that investors are seeking additional compensation for perceived risks associated with holding long-term government debt. What is notable is that, even with inflation appearing to decelerate and with some evidence that the economy is slowing (slow employment growth and slow retail sales growth), bond investors still expect higher returns. Moreover, expectations for monetary policy have shifted, with investors now seeing a high probability that the Fed will not raise rates in September and a high probability of only one rate hike before the end of the year. Despite the shift in sentiment toward a less tight monetary policy, investors want to be compensated for the risk of holding government bonds. US inflation eases * Inflation eased in July in the United States, although it remained far higher than it was prior to the start of the Middle East conflict. On the other hand, core (underlying) inflation fell to a level last seen just prior to the conflict. Not surprisingly, this latest data led to a decline in investor expectations for a tightening of monetary policy. Let’s look at the details: Energy prices are the key: In July, energy prices were up 14.7% from a year earlier and down 1.5% from the previous month. The year-to-year increase was the lowest since March, reflecting the easing of crude-oil prices following the temporary ceasefire in the Middle East. Meanwhile, the price of gasoline in the United States was up 24.6% in July versus a year earlier and down 2.9% from the previous month. Thus, although events in the Middle East led to some easing of energy prices, prices remain significantly above the level seen prior to the start of the conflict. The easing of US inflation coincided with a shift in expectations about monetary policy. At the time of writing, the futures market’s implied probability of the Federal Reserve hiking its benchmark interest rate next month was 37.9%—down from 48.4% a day before and 54.4% a week before. Indeed, with inflation easing and the job market weakening, the argument for increasing the interest rate is becoming less strong. On the other hand, the futures market’s implied probability of a rate hike before the end of the year is 72.5%. While down from yesterday and a week ago, this still indicates that investors anticipate a need to tighten monetary policy in the face of persistent inflation. Moreover, investors are likely concerned that inflation could rebound if the situation in the Middle East does not improve. What does the jobs report mean for monetary policy? The Federal Reserve has a dual mandate to seek low inflation and high employment. Inflation has been seen as the primary challenge given that it has persistently been above the Fed’s 2% target. Yet, the weakening labor market could become cause of concern for the Fed. Plus, a weakening labor market will likely lead to less inflationary pressure. As such, today’s report likely reduces the probability of a rate hike anytime soon. Indeed, following the release of today’s report, the futures market’s implied probability of a rate hike in September fell from 55% yesterday to 41.9% today. There are several potential explanations for the rise in CDS prices. First, there is increasing concern about tech companies’ ability to generate sufficient cash to cover debt-servicing costs. A major tech company reported its first quarter of negative free cash flow since it went public two decades ago. Moreover, bond yields have risen, and further tightening of monetary policy could push them higher, increasing the cost of servicing debts. Reserve on interest-rate policy were not a surprise. Usually, the direction of monetary policy was widely anticipated, often having been signaled by the Fed itself. This time is different, however. Prior to the announcement by the US Fed last week, the futures market was signaling an implied probability of 33% that the Fed would raise its benchmark rate that day, and a probability of 67% that the Fed would leave the rate unchanged. That indicates there was significant uncertainty in the minds of investors, which likely reflects the fact that Fed Chair Warsh did not previously offer a hint vis-a-vis his On July 29, 2026, the Federal Reserve’s Open Market Committee announced that the benchmark interest rate will remain unchanged. The 12-member committee voted 9-to-3 to keep the rate unchanged, with three members voting to boost the rate by 25 basis points. The committee commented that “economic activity is expanding at a solid pace despite elevated uncertainty that owes, in part, to the conflict in the Middle East. Productivity growth and capital investment are strong. Job gains have kept pace with the workforce, and the unemployment rate has changed little. Inflation remains elevated relative to the committee’s 2% goal, in part reflecting supply shocks that have driven price increases in certain sectors, including energy. The committee will deliver price stability.” In his press conference, Fed Chair Kevin Warsh reiterated that the Fed intends to maintain the 2% target for inflation, which he deemed the definition of price stability. Moreover, he said he wants to anchor investor expectations, that is, he wants to convince investors that the Fed intends to maintain the 2% target. Warsh also said that, if inflation remains elevated, interest rates could be “part of the equation” for the Fed in targeting lower inflation. However, Warsh was repeatedly asked by reporters why the Fed was not simply acting now to raise interest rates. His answer was that such impatience was not warranted. Meanwhile, investors evidently now expect the Fed to raise the benchmark rate at its next meeting in September. The futures market’s implied probability of a rate hike in September is now 68%. Plus, there is an implied probability of 89% that the Fed will raise the benchmark rate at least once before the end of the year, as well as a roughly 48% likelihood of two or more hikes before the end of the year. The expectation that the Fed will tighten monetary policy this year reflects concern that oil prices are likely to remain elevated or even rise further, mainly due to the risk of continued conflict in the Middle East. Following an Iranian attack on US facilities this week, the United States and Saudi Arabia attacked Iran-allied facilities in Iraq. These actions led to a sharp rebound in the price of oil. Following Warsh’s press conference, yields began to soar, with the yield on the 30-year bond hitting the highest level since 2007. Plus, the gap between the yields on 30-year and two-year bonds shot up by almost 20 basis points. Second, Warsh did not indicate an intention to raise rates. When discussing how the Fed would respond if inflation remains elevated, he said that interest rates were one “part of the equation,” suggesting that there might be other inflation-fighting tools—although he did not say what those tools might be. Moreover, he said that there could be indicators other than the personal consumption expenditures deflator for measuring inflation, yet he did not indicate what those indicators might be. Finally, he suggested that, by boosting yields, the market is already tightening monetary policy, thereby suggesting that the Fed might not need to do anything. Normally, a Fed meeting that leaves the benchmark interest rate unchanged means no news and no significant movement in asset prices. But this time, the situation was different. Although the benchmark rate remained unchanged, asset prices moved a lot, as comments from the chair evidently created uncertainty.

highlights: THE FEDERAL RESERVE (THE FED) ON SEPTEMBER 16 raised its federal funds rate by .25%, to between 3.75% to 4.00%, ending a stretch of cutting and holding going back more than three years. While disappointing for many investors, businesses and consumers, the hike was widely expected, with the economy humming, war-related energy prices up and inflation showing no signs of going away. August Consumer Price Index (CPI) overall numbers (including food and energy), announced September 11, remained stubbornly stuck at 3.4% year over year. 1 That news followed a surprising gain of 162,000 jobs in August. 2 And amid Iran war uncertainties, oil prices jumped to more than $100 per barrel for the first time since July. 3 Rate increases are the Fed’s primary tool for slowing things down when the economy and prices heat up. But they come at a cost — making borrowing more expensive for businesses and individuals, potentially slowing economic growth. BofA Global Research has forecast additional increases of .25% each, in October and December. “Expect heightened short-term volatility,” says Chris Hyzy, Chief Investment Officer for Merrill and Bank of America Private Bank. “But also long-term interest rates could come down slightly as bond investors become more comfortable with the Fed’s resolve.” Rate increases depress values for holders of existing bonds and could create turbulence for equity investors at a time when the Middle East and the coming midterm elections already pose volatility risks. THE FEDERAL RESERVE (THE FED) ON JULY 29 kept its federal funds rate at 3.50% to 3.75%. While rate expectations have broadly shifted from cuts to potential increases later this year, the Fed so far this year has held steady as it processes complex and sometimes mixed signals on the economy and inflation. Testifying before Congress on July 14, new Fed Chair Kevin Warsh underscored the Federal Open Market Committee’s commitment “to put these years of high inflation behind us.” 1 With the Iran war elevating energy costs and U.S. companies and consumers showing remarkable resilience, many analysts believe the Fed will soon raise rates to keep inflation from reigniting. BofA Global Research now expects three rate increases of .25% each in 2026, starting in September. Yet the Fed still faces a delicate balance. Lower-than-expected inflation 2 and employment figures 3 from June offered reminders of early 2026, when a seemingly slowing economy raised expectations of a cut. “Further rate decisions will be based on the Fed’s analysis of the latest information as it unfolds,” says Chris Hyzy, Chief Investment Officer for Merrill and Bank of America Private Bank. IN KEVIN WARSH’S FIRST MEETING AS FED CHAIR, the Federal Reserve (the Fed) on June 17 held the federal funds rate steady at 3.50% to 3.75%. The decision dashed any hopes that a change in leadership might prompt immediate rate-cutting and signaled that inflation is at least as big a concern for the Fed right now as stimulating economic growth. Just a week earlier, May’s Consumer Price Index (CPI) showed the annual inflation rate climbing above 4% for the first time in three years. 1 “Conditions have shifted from the start of the year, when two cuts for 2026 seemed likely,” says Chris Hyzy, Chief Investment Officer for Merrill and Bank of America Private Bank. The Iran war spiked energy costs and pushed prices for other goods higher, and the U.S. economy has shown remarkable resilience, adding 172,000 jobs in May. 2 Equity markets, despite heightened volatility, continue to find new highs, and long-term bond yields have risen amid investor concerns over the Middle East and inflation. 3 The administration supported Warsh as likelier than his predecessor, Jerome Powell, to push for lower rates, 4 which make borrowing easier and tend to stimulate hiring. Yet sticky inflation generally prompts the Fed to do the opposite, raising rates to slow the economy. “BofA Global Research now foresees no new rate cuts until at least mid-2027, and the chances of a .25% increase in the next year have grown,” Hyzy says. “Moving forward, new economic data will be the most important factor as the Fed balances its dual mandates of full employment and stable inflation.” May’s healthy jobs numbers, while good news for workers and the economy, helped drive a 2.6% drop in the S&P 500 index on June 5 as hopes of a rate cut diminished. 5 “Investors should expect that sort of choppiness over the next few months,” Hyzy believes. “Yet the job gains, spread across healthcare, logistics, financial services, hospitality and leisure and other industries, reflect strong economic fundamentals,” Hyzy adds. “Stay diversified and consider viewing short-term volatility as a potential opportunity to strategically add to your portfolio,” he suggests. LATEST TALKS BETWEEN IRAN AND THE U.S., if they succeed, could lead to a welcome opening of the Strait of Hormuz. The shutdown has caused history’s greatest oil disruption, affecting some 20% of the world’s supply. 1 So, how has the world thus far avoided an economic crisis? “While higher oil prices and inflation are creating real pain for millions of consumers, several factors have helped to limit its global impact so far,” says Ariana Chiu, investment strategist in the Chief Investment Office (CIO) for Merrill and Bank of America Private Bank. “A robust economy and energy self-sufficiency are supporting U.S. economic stability in the face of the Hormuz oil shock,” Chiu says. Asia, which accepts more than 80% of the oil that moves through the Strait of Hormuz, 2 and Europe, which sources much of its jet fuel via the passageway, are feeling the brunt, she adds. Yet the global economy has shown surprising resilience, thanks to several forces EVEN AS LEADERSHIP OF THE FEDERAL RESERVE (the Fed) changes hands, persistent inflation may eliminate chances of hoped-for interest rate cuts through 2026. Kevin Warsh, confirmed by the full Senate on May 13, replaces Jerome Powell, whose term as chair ends on May 15. While the administration backed Warsh, a so-called interest rate dove favoring lower rates, as potentially more aggressive than his predecessor in pushing for cuts, 1 April inflation figures released yesterday show the Consumer Price Index up 3.8% from a year ago, well above the Fed’s 2% target. 2 The latest inflation figures clearly present a challenge for the new Fed chair. Markets welcome interest rate cuts because they stimulate hiring and economic growth and make it easier for businesses and consumers to borrow money. “Yet while the labor market has softened, we haven’t seen an increase in recent layoffs,” says Matthew Diczok, head of Cross-Asset Market Strategy for the Chief Investment Office (CIO). “For the time being, this labor stability enables the Fed to focus on inflation pressures related to energy price spikes from the Iran conflict and tariff uncertainties, rather than unemployment.” Warsh would need to rally six other Fed governors to vote for a rate cut — a difficult task as long as these conditions persist, he adds. “Markets, in fact, no longer expect rate cuts this year. That’s not necessarily a bad thing, as it highlights continuing economic resilience. Should inflation slow, as expected, it likely just pushes rate cuts into 2027.” BofA Global Research, which had anticipated two cuts in 2026, now believes cuts may not come until mid or late 2027. A rate hike this year is considered unlikely. Today, productivity gains from artificial intelligence (AI) and other technologies are outpacing wage growth and supporting strong equity market performance, Diczok notes. “If productivity gains continue and we are able to work through the current energy crisis and get past tariff uncertainties, that would support the Fed’s ability to resume rate cuts next year.”

highlights: - The Federal Reserve (Fed) lifted their policy rate to 3.75%–4.00% amid a renewed focus on lowering inflation. - Rising oil prices drove inflation and Treasury yields higher so far this year. - Markets expect additional Federal Reserve rate hikes through mid-2027. The Federal Reserve (Fed) influences borrowing costs, savings returns and financial conditions across the economy. Congress directs the Fed to pursue maximum employment and stable prices, goals commonly known as its dual mandate. The Fed’s September decision renewed its emphasis on controlling inflation while employment and consumer spending remained resilient. At its September 16 meeting, the Federal Open Market Committee raised the federal funds target range by 0.25 percentage point to 3.75%–4.00%. The federal funds rate is the short-term rate banks charge one another for overnight loans of reserves, and changes can influence mortgages, credit cards, business loans, savings yields and bond markets. Investors largely expected the increase, which marked the first Federal Reserve rate hike in more than three years. Source: U.S. Federal Reserve, September 16, 2026. Current labor data indicate that the economy remains near maximum employment. The Bureau of Labor Statistics’ August employment report showed the unemployment rate standing at 4.1%, employers adding an average of 80,000 jobs each month this year and weekly initial jobless claims remaining near all-time lows. 1 These labor market conditions are allowing policymakers to focus more directly on inflation. The committee approved the rate increase unanimously after three members dissented at the prior meeting. The vote indicates that Chair Kevin Warsh built broader support for a firmer response to inflation. Before the announcement, market prices indicated about a 90% probability of an increase, and investors now anticipate three additional hikes by mid-2027, including one more in 2026. Warsh declined to submit projections for the Fed’s Summary of Economic Projections because he views those forecasts as a form of forward guidance. Excluding Warsh, the median policymaker forecast shows one additional rate increase in 2026, slightly stronger economic growth in 2027 and little change in next year’s inflation outlook. Policymakers also raised their 2028 inflation projection slightly, signaling that they expect price pressures to take time to settle. The Fed made few changes to its official policy statement added that “ Rate increases from 2022 through 2023 helped slow inflation, but higher oil costs have renewed near-term price pressure. Core Consumer Price Inflation rose 2.4% year-over-year in August, while Core Personal Consumption Expenditures (PCE) rose from 3.0% in December 2025 to 3.3% in July 2026. Headline PCE, which includes more volatile food and energy prices, rose 3.7% year-over-year in July, well above the Fed’s 2% target and strengthens the case for tighter policy. 2 Sources: U.S. Bank Asset Management Group Research, Bloomberg; August 31, 2021 – August 31, 2026. West Texas Intermediate crude oil futures started the year near $57 per barrel, peaked at $113 in April and recently moved back above $100. Higher energy costs can raise transportation, manufacturing and household expenses, which may spread inflation across the economy. Oil’s renewed rise has increased expectations for additional rate hikes and lifted both short- and long-term Treasury yields. 3 Central banks outside the United States face similar inflation pressure from higher energy prices. The European Central Bank and Bank of Japan have already raised rates in 2026, and investors expect the Bank of England and Bank of Canada to follow. This broad shift reverses the 2025 easing cycle and could keep global borrowing costs elevated. Interest-rate decisions represent only one part of Fed policy. The Fed also influences financial conditions through its balance sheet, which includes Treasury securities and other bond holdings. Those holdings stand near $6.6 trillion after peaking near $9 trillion in 2022, and the Fed stopped shrinking the balance sheet in December 2025. The Fed began buying short-term Treasury bills in December 2025 to maintain ample bank reserves and keep overnight rates near its target. These purchases absorb part of the Treasury supply available to investors and can improve market liquidity, meaning the amount of money readily available to buy goods, services and financial assets. The Fed has reduced its regular purchases in 2026, and its holdings have changed little since Warsh became chair. Ample liquidity can help financial markets absorb unexpected shocks and function smoothly. Balance-sheet policy cannot remove the economic risks created by inflation, higher energy costs or geopolitical conflict, and Warsh has questioned whether large-scale purchases remain appropriate over the long term. He has formed a task force to review the Fed’s approach to data, communication and balance-sheet policy. Investors should evaluate Federal Reserve asset purchases interest rates, economic growth rather than rely on a single policy signal. A larger balance sheet can improve liquidity higher policy rates restrain borrowing and demand. These tools can work in different directions because the Fed uses each one to address a distinct part of market functioning or the economy. We maintain a constructive outlook for diversified portfolios and see opportunities in U.S. stocks, global infrastructure and structured credit, or investments backed by pools of loans and other debt. Higher energy costs could lift inflation and slow economic activity, but consumer spending and corporate earnings remain resilient. Lower corporate and individual taxes and recent tariff rebates also provide fiscal support to the economy. Fed policy will continue to respond to new evidence on inflation, employment, consumer demand and energy prices. Current conditions support a restrictive stance, but incoming economic data will shape the path ahead. A long-term plan can separate temporary market noise from developments that truly change the long-term outlook. The Federal Open Market Committee unanimously raised the federal funds target range by 0.25 percentage point to 3.75%–4.00%. The increase marked the first Fed rate hike in more than three years. Policymakers emphasized their commitment to returning inflation to the 2% target while consumer spending and employment remained resilient. Persistent inflation and higher oil prices strengthened the case for tighter monetary policy. Core Personal Consumption Expenditures inflation, which excludes volatile food and energy prices, rose from 3.0% in December 2025 to 3.3% in July 2026. Higher energy costs can also spread through transportation, production and household expenses, adding to broader price pressure. Market prices and the median Fed policymaker projection point to another rate increase in 2026, with investors anticipating three additional hikes by mid-2027. The path remains conditional rather than fixed because inflation, employment, consumer demand and oil prices can change. The Fed may adjust the pace or direction of policy as new economic data arrive.

results.title: Disagreement about Monetary Policy
highlights: Disagreement about Monetary Policy This paper studies why central banks and markets hold different beliefs. I introduce a model that formalizes three mechanisms for disagreement: asymmetric information about fundamentals, different perceptions of the policy rule, and different confidence in public signals. I show how to separately identify these mechanisms using their predictions for beliefs about multiple variables. In US data, negative macroeconomic news predicts market overestimation of interest rates and employment relative to realizations and Federal Reserve forecasts. The estimates imply that markets slightly misspecify the monetary rule and are significantly underconfident in public information. Central bank private information and “information effects” are quantitatively negligible. (JEL D82, D83, E24, E43, E52, E58) - Nina Karnaukh, Petra Vokatá. results.title: Does U.S. Monetary Policy Respond to Macroeconomic Uncertainty?
highlights: We find that macroeconomic uncertainty plays a significant role in U.S. monetary policy. First, we construct a measure of uncertainty as felt by policymakers at the time of making their ratesetting decisions. This measure is derived from a real-time, Bayesian estimation of a small monetary VAR with time-varying parameters. We use it to calculate the probability of being in a high-uncertainty regime. Second, we estimate a monetary policy reaction function that, apart from macroeconomic uncertainty, includes Greenbook forecasts, revisions of those forecasts, and a measure of stock market volatility. Using data for the period 1969 -2008, we find that policymakers set an interest rate that is significantly lower in a high-uncertainty regime, compared to a low-uncertainty regime. Monetary policymakers often emphasize the importance of uncertainty. Greenspan (2004) , for example, notes that "uncertainty is not just a pervasive feature of the monetary policy landscape; it is the defining characteristic of that landscape" (p. 36). Uncertainty has also been proposed as an important driver of business cycles (e.g., Bloom et al., 2018; Caldara et al., 2016) . The idea is that uncertainty causes cautious behaviour by consumers and firms, leading to decreasing output and increasing unemployment. 1 To counteract these effects, monetary policy should be looser in high-uncertainty regimes. 2 Uncertainty has resurfaced in the monetary policy debate in the context of the COVID-19 pandemic (e.g., Panetta, 2020) . Following Romer and Romer (2004) , we estimate the reaction function meeting by meeting. Compared to a monthly or quarterly specification, this has the advantage that it prevents endogeneity issues related to the impact of monetary policy on uncertainty that is evidenced by Mumtaz and Theodoridis (2019) : at the meeting frequency there is simply no time for the policy decisions to affect uncertainty. Our baseline sample covers FOMC meetings in the period 1969 -2008. We also estimate policy reaction functions separately on the periods 1969 -1979 and 1987 -2008. We have three main results. First, U.S. monetary policy is significantly affected by macroeconomic uncertainty. On the full sample, the linear response to a one-standarddeviation increase in macroeconomic uncertainty is a decrease in the intended funds rate of 7 basis points. Second, we find that instead of a linear response, the role of macroeconomic uncertainty is best captured in terms of low-and high-uncertainty regimes. The Fed sets a funds rate that is 14 basis points lower in a high-uncertainty regime than in a lowuncertainty regime. When calculating the probability of being in a high-uncertainty regime with output or inflation uncertainty, the differences between the two regimes are 17 and 16 basis points, respectively. Third, financial uncertainty, as proxied by the VXO index, plays a significant role in monetary policy that is separate from the one played by macroeconomic uncertainty. On the full sample, a one-standard-deviation increase in the VXO index is associated with a decrease in the intended funds rate of 4.3 basis points. Most importantly for our analysis, we include financial and macroeconomic uncertainty in the monetary policy reaction function. Including both allows us to disentangle the response to financial uncertainty, which has already been established in the literature, from that to macroeconomic uncertainty. The VXO at the time of meeting m is denoted by VXO m . We consider several variants of the reaction function that differ in terms of the macroeconomic uncertainty measure (U m ) that is included. Our main specification uses the entropy measure of aggregate uncertainty (U m = U M m ), but we also estimate the reaction to uncertainty related to output growth (U m = U ym ) and inflation (U m = U πm ). We do not consider interest rate uncertainty, because funds rate forecasts are not as relevant for monetary policymakers (since they are the ones who determine the future rate). In Figure 2 , we plot the resulting entropy-based macroeconomic uncertainty measure, together with the VXO index, which we use as financial uncertainty proxy. First, and most importantly for our analysis, there seems to be no clear relationship between the two types of uncertainty. results.title: State-Dependent Sticky Expectations: Evidence and Theory
highlights: We document novel stylized facts regarding updating of households' inflation expectations. Using two randomized controlled trials fielded in the US and Germany where signals in the form of professionals' inflation forecasts have different perceived levels of precision, we show that households react more to information with higher levels of precision, in line with Bayesian updating. However, in contrast to Bayesian updating, they mostly respond differently to these signals in the decision to update expectations (extensive margin) and not in the size of the adjustment (intensive margin). The extensive margin also displays a pronounced asymmetry: Households more frequently update their expectations when the signal is above the prior compared to when the signal is below the prior. We propose a model where households' inflation expectations exhibit state-dependent inattentiveness to inflation signals. In times of high uncertainty, elevated inflation expectations may persist due to the increased information processing costs of uncertain inflation signals and the relatively smaller welfare losses of not adjusting expectations when signals are below priors (disinflations) compared to when signals are above priors (accelerating inflation). Our model provides microfoundations for the asymmetric loss function that is commonly assumed to explain biases in inflation expectations. - Financial Literacy, Pension, Retirement Analysis - Decision-Making and Behavioral Economics - Monetary Policy and Economic Impact - Olivier Coibion, Yuriy Gorodnichenko, Michael Weber. results.title: Is the Intrinsic Value of Macroeconomic News Announcements Related to Their Asset Price Impact?
highlights: The literature documents a heterogeneous asset price response to macroeconomic news announcements. We explain this variation with a novel measure of the intrinsic value of an announcement - the announcement's ability to nowcast GDP growth, inflation, and the Federal Funds Target Rate - and decompose it into the announcement's relation to fundamentals, a timeliness premium, and a revision premium. We find that differences in intrinsic value can explain a significant fraction of the variation in the announcements' price impact on Treasury bond yields. Prior to the release, an early median of analysts had seen core PCE at 0.24-0.25% M/M, similar to 0.25% in July; it had been around 0.21-0.22% pre-PPI; consensus now appears to be clustered in the high 0.20s.

results.title: Big Bank Earnings Meet a Key CPI Report: What to Watch This Week as the S&P 500 Hovers Near Records - Liberty Markets.us
highlights: JPMorgan, Goldman Sachs, Citigroup and Wells Fargo report today, and September CPI lands Wednesday, with the 10-year yield near 5.2% and the Fed meeting two weeks out. Here is what the data and strategists say to watch. Matt Hardy October 13, 2026 7 minutes read This is the first big test of third-quarter earnings season and of the inflation data that will shape the Fed’s next move. JPMorgan Chase, Goldman Sachs, Citigroup and Wells Fargo report before the open today (Tuesday, October 13), with Morgan Stanley and Bank of America due Wednesday, according to a Reuters week-ahead preview. The September CPI report is also due Wednesday, October 14. Reuters’ poll expects headline CPI of 3.6% year over year and core CPI of 2.5%, while the 10-year Treasury yield sits around 5.23%, near its highest level in 24 years. The Fed meets October 27-28, after raising rates in September for the first time since 2023. Results were not yet known at the time of writing, so this article focuses on what to watch rather than what happened. Per Reuters, the S&P 500 hit an all-time closing high last Tuesday, its first since mid-August, and is up more than 13% year to date despite declines on Wednesday and Thursday. Reuters also notes that LSEG IBES expects third-quarter S&P 500 earnings to grow more than 30%, following a strong first half. Our own coverage of the prior quarter is in S&P 500 Q2 2026 Earnings: Strongest Growth Since 2021, which provides useful context for how high the earnings bar has become. The weak spot is financials. Reuters reports the S&P 500 banks index fell about 9% over the past month, among the market’s weakest groups as Treasury yields rose. That sets up an unusual dynamic: the sector reporting first is also the one carrying the most skepticism. The September CPI report arrives Wednesday, October 14. The Reuters poll points to 3.6% annual headline inflation and 2.5% core, against the Fed’s 2% target. A separate consensus compiled by MarketWatch and cited by Stocktwits is slightly different, at +0.6% month over month and 3.7% year over year for headline, and +0.2% month over month and 2.5% year over year for core. The gap between forecasts is small, but it is a reminder that “consensus” is not one number. The headline-versus-core gap is the story. A headline reading well above core points to energy as a major driver, which fits the oil-driven volatility we have covered in Stocks Rebound Sharply the Day After the Fed’s Rate Hike. Reuters adds that producer price and retail sales reports are also due this week. According to Reuters, traders have reduced bets on another rate hike at the October 27-28 meeting, but hotter data could revive them. Matt Stucky, chief portfolio manager for equities at Northwestern Mutual Wealth Management, said: “If you start to see more evidence of re-accelerating inflation that’s not going to come down absent a full hiking cycle from the Fed, that’s where equity markets really can be under pressure.” Michael Reynolds of Glenmede put the focus on services: “We really want to see material progress on (core services inflation) to get a little bit more confident that the Fed doesn’t have to be as aggressive as maybe the market’s pricing in,” adding that “at some point, major indices are going to cry uncle on higher rates.” Stocktwits also notes that Kevin Warsh is scheduled to speak Thursday at the IMF and World Bank annual meetings, and that Cleveland Fed President Beth Hammack has a speaking engagement the same day. Reuters says the 10-year yield was around 5.23% late last week. Many investors had treated 5% as a key threshold for stock market pressure, yet the market has so far absorbed yields above that level. We examined the rate backdrop in Stocks Slide as 10-Year Treasury Yield Hits Highest Level Since 2007. A hot CPI print could test how durable that tolerance is, while a benign one could ease pressure on rate-sensitive sectors, including banks. Reuters says it is due Wednesday, October 14. The Reuters poll expects 3.6% headline and 2.5% core inflation year over year. The Fed raised rates in September and meets again October 27-28. Hotter inflation data could revive bets on another hike, which strategists quoted by Reuters flag as a risk for equities.

highlights: * Fed’s Hammack sounds hawkish, Middle-East tensions escalate * Oil prices revive inflation fears, but Fed bets steady ahead of US CPI data * RBA leaves door open to additional hikes, BoJ expected to hike gradually * Wall Street trades cautiously as major US banks kick off earnings season The US dollar strengthened against all its major peers on Monday, driven by hawkish Fed commentary and renewed tensions in the Middle East. Today, the greenback is pulling back, perhaps as traders are adjusting their positions ahead of the resumption of Treasury trading today and the US CPI data tomorrow. Cleveland Fed President Beth Hammack sounded hawkish yesterday, warning that inflation expectations could become less anchored if policymakers delay in taking action and suggesting that the neutral rate may be higher than previously estimated. Her comments came as oil prices rebounded amid new tensions and strikes in the Middle East and Ukraine. With the reopening of the Strait of Hormuz becoming a far-fetched dream once again and Russia carrying out strikes on Ukraine, including damage to a thermal power plant in Kharkiv, thereby violating the proposed energy ceasefire, oil prices rebounded, intensifying inflation fears once again. Having said all that though, investors’ expectations about the future course of the Fed’s actions have not been impacted. Market participants still assign a 20% chance of an October hike, fully pricing in the move for December. By the end of 2027, a total of 80bps worth of hikes is baked into the cake. Today, two more Fed officials will step onto the rostrum: Richmond Fed President Thomas Barkin and Boston Fed President Susan Collins. It will be interesting to see whether they share Hamack’s hawkish views or lean towards those of Vice Fed Chair Jefferson and New York Fed President Williams, who have suggested that the Committee should not rush into pressing the hike button too soon. As for tomorrow’s CPI inflation data, both the S&P Global and ISM price-related subindices suggest that the risks may be tilted to the upside. Therefore, hotter-than-expected prints could add more fuel to the dollar’s engines, even if they don’t significantly boost the chances of an October hike. They could add more basis points worth of rate hikes for next year. Elsewhere, the minutes of the latest RBA meeting revealed that policymakers believed the upside inflation risks identified earlier had already materialized or started building, leaving the door open to another rate increase if inflation proves more persistent than expected. The probability of another rate hike before the turn of the year continues to hover near 50%. A strong employment report on Thursday could take that probability higher. The International Monetary Fund (IMF) said today that the Bank of (BoJ) likely raise interest setting, despite an expected slowdown in growth On Wall Street, both the S&P 500 and the Nasdaq closed slightly in the red on Monday, with only the Dow Jones adding some gains. Perhaps the reason why there was no material decline following Hammack’s remarks was the anticipated start of the bank earnings season later today. JPMorgan (NYSE: JPM), Goldman Sachs (NYSE: GS), Citigroup (NYSE: C) and Wells Fargo are all due to report today, followed by Bank of America and Morgan Stanley on Wednesday. results.title: US CPI Surprise: Temporary Relief for Rates? DBS Experts Analyze (2026)
highlights: If you’ve been following the economic headlines, you’ve likely seen the recent buzz about the softer-than-expected June CPI data in the United States. On the surface, it looks like a win—inflation easing, pressure on the Fed to hike rates subsiding, and markets breathing a sigh of relief. But personally, I think this narrative is a bit too simplistic. What makes this particularly fascinating is how quickly the markets reacted, with the US Treasuries curve bull steepening as yields adjusted to the cooler-than-expected numbers. Yet, if you take a step back and think about it, this might just be a temporary blip rather than a fundamental shift. The headline and core CPI figures came in at -0.4% and 0.0% month-over-month, respectively, both below consensus estimates. One thing that immediately stands out is the 5.7% decline in energy prices, which was the biggest drag on the overall index. But here’s where it gets interesting: core services prices (excluding shelter) also dropped by 0.4%. What this really suggests is that inflationary pressures might not be as widespread as feared—at least for now. However, what many people don’t realize is that the AI boom is driving up prices in the computer software and accessories sector, which could be a wildcard in the months ahead. From my perspective, the market’s reaction to these numbers feels a bit knee-jerk. Yes, the data was softer, but it doesn’t change the broader economic landscape. The US economy remains resilient, equities are strong, and oil prices are creeping back up. In my opinion, this CPI print is more of a speed bump than a roadblock for the Fed. The softer CPI data has pushed Fed tightening bets toward the end of the year, with July effectively off the table. But here’s the catch: the Fed isn’t just looking at inflation in isolation. They’re also weighing the strength of the labor market, consumer spending, and global economic conditions. A detail that I find especially interesting is how quickly market participants shifted to a ‘pay-on-dip’ mode, as if the inflation fight is already won. What this really suggests is that investors are still chasing yields in a low-rate environment, even as the Fed tries to navigate a delicate balance. Personally, I think the Fed will remain cautious, especially with oil prices rising and the potential for inflation to resurge. The question is: how long can this ‘temporary relief’ last? If there’s one thing I’ve learned from watching economic cycles, it’s that inflation is stubborn. It doesn’t disappear overnight, and it rarely stays dormant for long. The current dip in CPI is largely driven by energy prices, which are notoriously volatile. What makes this particularly fascinating is how quickly narratives can shift. Just a few months ago, everyone was talking about persistent inflation; now, it’s all about disinflation. But here’s the broader perspective: the US economy is still firing on many cylinders. Strong equities, robust consumer spending, and a tight labor market all point to underlying inflationary pressures. In my opinion, the Fed’s job isn’t done—it’s just paused. The real test will come when energy prices stabilize or rise again, and we see how sticky core inflation really is. The markets seem to be in a ‘wait-and-see’ mode, but I think there’s more to it. The resurgence in oil prices, coupled with the AI-driven tech boom, could reignite inflation concerns faster than many expect. One thing that immediately stands out is how quickly sentiment can shift. Just as the markets celebrated the cool CPI numbers, they could just as easily reverse course if the data turns hotter again. From my perspective, the key will be how the Fed communicates its next steps. If they signal a more dovish stance, it could fuel risk-taking and potentially stoke inflation further. But if they maintain a hawkish tone, it could dampen growth and keep inflation in check—at least for a while. The softer CPI data is undoubtedly good news, but it’s not a game-changer. What many people don’t realize is that inflation is a complex beast, influenced by everything from global supply chains to technological advancements. Personally, I think this moment of relief is an opportunity to reassess the bigger picture. If you take a step back and think about it, the real story isn’t the CPI numbers themselves—it’s what they imply about the economy’s resilience and the Fed’s ongoing challenge. This raises a deeper question: are we truly out of the inflation woods, or is this just a temporary lull before the next wave? Only time will tell, but one thing is certain—the inflation fight is far from over.

results.title: US Hiring Stalls in September as Unemployment Climbs to 4.2%, Undercutting Case for a Fed Rate Hike - Journalism Central
highlights: The American job market cooled sharply in September, with employers adding just 29,000 positions, far short of the roughly 84,000 to 90,000 that economists polled by Reuters and Dow Jones had expected. The Bureau of Labor Statistics, which released the figures on October 2, also reported that the unemployment rate ticked up to 4.2% from 4.1% in August, leaving about 7.1 million Americans officially out of work. The report lands at a delicate moment for the economy, with the Federal Reserve weighing its next move on interest rates and households already squeezed by inflation running above wage growth. The size of the miss is what rattled economists most. A gain of 29,000 jobs is barely a third of the weakest consensus estimate, and it continues a pattern of deceleration that has defined 2026’s labor market. The unemployment rate’s rise to 4.2% keeps it within the narrow 4.1% to 4.3% band it has occupied since March, but the direction of travel — upward — is unmistakable. BLS data show nonfarm payrolls essentially stalled, a marked change from the steadier, if unspectacular, hiring pace that characterized the first half of the year. Health care remained the labor market’s most reliable engine, adding 17,000 jobs in September. Even that was a slowdown; health care had averaged 33,000 new jobs a month over the prior year, according to BLS data. The weakness was concentrated elsewhere. Financial activities shed 7,000 jobs, the sharpest decline of any major sector, and insurance-related employment alone has fallen by 90,000 positions since May 2025, a sign that higher interest rates and consolidation in that industry are continuing to bite. Manufacturing and other goods-producing sectors showed little momentum either way, leaving the overall headline number dependent almost entirely on a shrinking health care contribution. Beyond the weak September print, the Labor Department also revised down its estimates for July and August by a combined 60,000 jobs. August’s previously reported gain of 162,000 was cut to just 133,000, and July’s already-modest increase of 21,000 was revised into an outright decline of 10,000 jobs. Those revisions matter because they strip away what had looked like a late-summer rebound, suggesting the underlying hiring trend has been weaker for longer than initially reported. Thomas Simons, chief U.S. economist at Jefferies, argued that August’s bounce was itself only a recovery from very weak hiring in June and July, not a genuine reacceleration. Average hourly earnings rose 3% over the past year, according to the BLS report, but that trails the 3.4% inflation rate recorded in the same period, meaning most workers’ paychecks are losing purchasing power in real terms even as nominal wages rise. That combination — slowing job growth and inflation-adjusted wage declines — is precisely the stagflation-adjacent mix that makes the Federal Reserve’s task more difficult, since weak hiring normally argues for lower rates while above-target inflation argues for higher ones. The report arrived only weeks after the Fed, now led by Chair Kevin Warsh following his contentious Senate confirmation in May, raised its benchmark rate in September for the first time since 2023, citing persistent inflation pressure. Simons said the September jobs data “should be the nail in the coffin for an October hike,” reflecting a view widely shared on trading desks that a central bank already worried about a softening labor market would be reluctant to tighten further and risk accelerating job losses. Markets, according to multiple reports following the release, sharply cut their odds of an October rate increase in response to the data. Not everyone reads the numbers the same way, however; some Fed officials have continued to emphasize that headline inflation remains well above the 2% target and that a single soft jobs report, especially one still showing positive — if weak — payroll growth, does not by itself justify abandoning a tightening bias. The September report leaves the Fed boxed in between two unattractive scenarios: tightening further into a visibly cooling labor market, or holding steady while inflation stays elevated. Whichever path policymakers choose, the data suggests the labor market’s soft patch is broader than a single weak month, given the sizable downward revisions to July and August. Economists will be watching the October employment report, due November 6, closely for confirmation of whether September’s weakness was an aberration tied to seasonal hiring patterns or the start of a more sustained slowdown. For households, the immediate consequence is clear regardless of the Fed’s next move: with wage growth trailing inflation and job creation thin, the squeeze on real incomes that defined much of 2026 shows no sign of easing soon.

results.title: US Hiring Grinds to a Near-Halt as September Payrolls Add Just 29,000 Jobs, a Third of What Was Forecast - Times of Capital
highlights: US employers added just 29,000 jobs in September, far below the roughly 90,000 economists expected, while unemployment rose to 4.2% and wage growth slowed to its weakest pace since 2021. The report, the last before the November 3 midterms, has economists split on whether the labor market is simply cooling or heading toward real trouble. By manvir · October 13, 2026 The US labor market delivered its clearest warning sign in months on Friday, October 2, when the Bureau of Labor Statistics reported that employers added just 29,000 jobs in September — roughly a third of the approximately 90,000 economists polled by Reuters and LSEG had expected, and well below the 84,000 consensus cited by Dow Jones. The unemployment rate ticked up to 4.2%, and revisions to prior months erased a combined 60,000 jobs from July and August, turning what had looked like a merely soft summer into a more sustained slowdown. It was not just the headline number that disappointed. Average hourly earnings rose only 0.1% month-over-month, against expectations of 0.3%, and just 3% year-over-year versus a forecast 3.2% — the slowest pace of wage growth since May 2021. Navy Federal Credit Union chief economist Heather Long summed up the composition of the gains bluntly, noting that “only healthcare and construction were hiring, and it was weak.” With most other sectors flat or shedding workers, the report pointed to a labor market losing breadth as well as speed. The weak print lands against an unusual backdrop: the Federal Reserve had just raised its benchmark rate by a quarter point, to a range of 3.75% to 4%, at its September 16 meeting — its first increase since 2023, taken to guard against inflation pressures even as employment growth was already cooling. That combination of a tightening central bank and a softening jobs market is precisely the kind of policy tension that tends to unsettle both bond and equity investors, since it raises the question of whether the Fed moved at the wrong moment in the cycle. The unemployment rate has now drifted in a narrow 4.1%-to-4.3% band since March, suggesting the slowdown has been building gradually rather than arriving as a sudden shock. Reactions from Wall Street economists ranged from cautious to alarmed. Jerry Tempelman, vice president of economic and fixed income research at Mutual of America, said the weak gain “raises questions about the durability of the labor market” following the Fed’s rate increase, framing the report as evidence the economy may not be able to absorb tighter policy as easily as hoped. Thomas Simons, chief US economist at Jefferies, was more pointed, calling the report “the nail in the coffin” for any chance of a further rate increase at the Fed’s next meeting. That divergence — one economist flagging structural fragility, another treating it mainly as a signal for near-term Fed policy — captures the uncertainty now hanging over the data. Timing has sharpened the report’s impact. It was the last monthly jobs release before the November 3 midterm elections, giving the weak numbers outsized political weight at a moment when voters are already weighing the economy’s performance. Coverage of the report noted it handed a headwind to the administration heading into the vote, with the mismatch between a tightening Fed and a cooling jobs market becoming a live talking point in the campaign’s closing weeks. The report immediately reshaped expectations for the Federal Reserve’s next policy meeting, scheduled for October 28. Futures markets had already been paring back the odds of additional tightening before the report; a print this weak makes the case for a pause even stronger, according to economists like Simons. For workers, the practical signal is a labor market that is still adding jobs but can no longer be counted on to do so briskly, with wage growth too slow to meaningfully outpace the cost of living. The next several payroll reports, and how the Fed weighs them against its inflation mandate at the October 28 meeting, will determine whether September marks a turning point toward a more serious slowdown or merely a rough patch in an otherwise resilient economy.

results.title: Fed Rate Hike in October? CPI Could Force Warsh's Hand - TNN
highlights: A Fed rate hike at the October 27–28 meeting looks unlikely, but not impossible, and Wednesday’s inflation report will say which way the risk tilts. Officials have spent two weeks signaling patience. Futures traders put the odds of an October increase near 20%, down from about 70% before Fed leaders began urging patience. Yet a hot reading on September consumer prices, driven by energy and watched closely for spillover into core goods and services, could revive the case for a second hike in a row. results.title: Fed Officials Turn Hawkish; US Dollar Index Eyes 103 Amid Highs | FXBrokerTrust
highlights: The US Dollar Index held near a yearly high of 102.61 on 13 October as Treasury yields eased to around 5.20%. ING analysts say markets are focused on US growth, elevated inflation and the prospect of 75 basis points in further rate hikes. Although US bond markets were closed for a holiday, the US Dollar Index showed remarkable resilience during the 12 October 2026 trading session, holding firmly at elevated levels and extending its strength in the following day's European session. Behind this lies robust US economic data, persistent inflationary pressure, and deep market expectations regarding the Federal Reserve's policy path. Market experts broadly agree that the outlook for the dollar remains positive, underpinned by the US economy's solid growth, persistently elevated inflation, and firm expectations that the Federal Reserve will adopt a more aggressive policy path. Analysts at ING noted that the foreign exchange market is currently filtering out recent short-term noise and refocusing on the key cyclical narratives: - Solid US economic growth; - Inflation running above target; - The broad prospect of the Federal Reserve raising rates by a further 75 basis points from current levels. Upcoming macroeconomic data will serve as a litmus test for market sentiment. Investors are closely watching the US September CPI and PPI figures, due for release on the evenings of 14 and 15 October, which are expected to have a profound impact on future interest rate expectations. Several regional Fed presidents have also issued clear guidance, noting that inflationary concerns remain elevated and that further rate hikes will be necessary to keep price pressures under control. Among the many statements from regional Fed presidents, remarks by Hammack stood out for their strikingly hawkish stance and drew widespread market attention. According to data from the FXS Speechtracker, Hammack's speech scored 8.4, well above the historical average of 7.5, clearly indicating that her push for policy tightening goes far beyond the conventional baseline. Hammack stated that, in order to force inflation down to the 2% policy target, the Federal Reserve must maintain a restrictive policy stance and keep benchmark interest rates at higher levels. Hammack further noted that, against a backdrop of broadly neutral financial conditions, demand-driven price pressures are spreading widely, even extending to emerging sectors such as artificial intelligence. She expressed concern that an inflationary mindset is gradually becoming entrenched, and warned that some companies are planning to raise end-product prices further beyond basic input costs, which undoubtedly heightens the risk of inflation becoming anchored. She stressed that the Federal Reserve should adopt a strategy of swift, incremental rate adjustments to act pre-emptively, preventing inflation expectations from spiralling further out of control and stopping inflation from becoming an intractable problem. Meanwhile, the FXS Fed Sentiment Index jumped sharply by 0.59 points to a high of 138.92, remaining firmly within hawkish territory. This strong rise clearly reflects that policymaker rhetoric is tilting decisively towards tightening, further reinforcing the broad consensus that, in the current market tug-of-war, the Federal Reserve will prioritise curbing inflation, with the policy balance favouring price control over shoring up economic growth.

results.title: Fed's Waller: Surging Treasury Yields Reflect Growth and AI Investment, Not Inflation
highlights: - Fed Governor Christopher Waller said rising long-term Treasury yields are driven by strong economic growth and AI-related investment, not inflation expectations. - He warned that weaker safe-haven demand for U.S. debt could be adding 50–70 basis points to yields, though that figure is attributed to Waller and not independently verified. - Waller expects the AI investment boom to continue for another 2–3 years, but he still sees inflation as too high and further rate hikes may be needed if data warrant. Rising U.S. Treasury yields are not a warning sign of unanchored inflation expectations, according to Federal Reserve Governor Christopher Waller. Instead, they reflect a powerful combination of robust economic growth and an artificial intelligence investment boom that is soaking up capital, he said Tuesday at Bloomberg’s New Economy Forum in New Delhi. Speaking to an audience of global financiers, Waller argued that the surge in long-term borrowing costs—which has pushed 10-year Treasury yields to multi-year highs—is largely a function of stronger growth prospects and increased competition for funding from AI infrastructure projects. He also pointed to a diminished safe-haven premium for U.S. government debt, which he estimated could be adding 50 to 70 basis points to yields. That estimate, attributed to Waller, has not been independently confirmed by market data. Waller’s remarks come at a delicate moment for monetary policy. The Fed raised its benchmark rate by 25 basis points in September to a range of 3.75%–4.00%, ending a nine-month pause. In an October 8 speech, Waller said inflation remained “too high” and that additional increases would likely be needed if incoming data followed his expectations. The latest reading of core personal consumption expenditures inflation showed a 3% annual rate—well above the Fed’s 2% target. Yet Waller’s tone on Tuesday suggested that higher long-term yields are already doing some of the Fed’s work. He specifically noted that interest-sensitive sectors like housing and automobiles are cooling, which could reduce the need for further policy tightening. The distinction is important: Waller is not signaling a pause, but he is acknowledging that market forces are providing some restraint. Waller’s argument that AI investment is driving yields higher rests on a simple premise: massive capital expenditures for data centers, semiconductors, and energy infrastructure are competing for a limited pool of savings, pushing real interest rates up. That dynamic, in turn, supports higher Treasury yields even if inflation expectations remain anchored. But the Fed governor also acknowledged that the AI boom is contributing to inflation in specific corners of the economy. In his October speech, he flagged that AI-driven demand for high-tech components—such as advanced chips and servers—has pushed up prices for those goods. He also cited elevated energy costs and potential new tariffs as obstacles to disinflation. The tension is clear: AI spending supports growth, but it also raises financing costs for the very investments that are fueling that growth. Reuters (TRI) reported in September that persistent inflation and further Fed tightening could materially affect AI capital expenditure plans. So far, however, there is little evidence of a slowdown. Waller said he expects the AI investment cycle to continue for another two to three years—a forecast that, like his yield estimate, is attributed to him and not independently verified. Markets will be watching incoming inflation and employment data to see if Waller’s growth-led explanation holds. The next Fed meeting is scheduled for December, and while no change is expected, the central bank’s statement and updated projections will be scrutinized for any shift in the reaction function. For now, Waller’s message is clear: the bond market is not flashing an inflation warning; it is responding to a world of stronger growth, massive AI investment, and a diminished safety premium. Whether that narrative survives the next round of data is an open question.

results.title: Fed Inflation Fight: Jobs, Wages and a Steadier US Consumer
highlights: The Federal Reserve faces an economy that looks oddly balanced. Unemployment is low enough to count as full employment, while wage growth is losing momentum 1. Inflation, meanwhile, is running at 3.4%, a figure that keeps price stability at the center of the central bank's agenda 2. Taken together, these conditions suggest a Fed that can concentrate on inflation without much fear of tipping the labor market into distress. That is the argument from Schwab's Henry Hoenig, who frames the combination of solid employment and cooling pay as giving policymakers room to keep fighting prices 1. Deloitte's consumer research describes the moment more cautiously, as a Fed "at a crossroads," and pairs that 3.4% inflation reading with what it characterizes as weak jobs 2. The most interesting tension is over the labor market. Schwab's view is that a jobless rate consistent with full employment is a source of strength, giving the Fed room to maneuver 1. Deloitte's framing of "weak jobs" points to more fragility 2. These positions aren't necessarily contradictory. A low unemployment rate can coexist with soft hiring momentum, and cooling wage growth can be read either as healthy normalization or as an early sign of a labor market losing steam. Which interpretation holds matters a great deal for policy. If the job market is merely settling into balance, the Fed can stay focused on bringing inflation down. If it is weakening, the central bank may soon have to weigh its inflation goal against rising employment risks. That second scenario is what a crossroads implies. On wages specifically, the outlook favors inflation fighters. Slower pay growth reduces the risk of a wage-price spiral, where rising labor costs feed into higher prices and vice versa. That is a key reason Schwab sees the current mix as giving the Fed flexibility 1. If the labor picture is debatable, the consumer picture is somewhat clearer: households appear to have found firmer footing. Deloitte's ConsumerSignals tracking shows its financial well-being index at 103.4 in August, the third consecutive month within a tight range, after sharper swings earlier in 2026 2. Spending intentions are also improving. Plans for discretionary purchases rose for a second straight month, reaching their strongest level since January 2026 2. Intentions for nondiscretionary spending ticked up too, which Deloitte reads as a sign of broader willingness to spend across categories rather than a shift between them 2. Price expectations remain elevated but show some relief. Seventy-one percent of respondents still expect grocery prices to rise, unchanged from the prior reading, while the share anticipating higher gas prices fell six points to 69% 2. Fuel costs are among the most visible prices for households, so easing gas expectations could help keep broader inflation expectations from becoming entrenched, something the Fed watches closely. For the Fed, stabilizing consumers cut both ways. Steadier finances and recovering spending intentions reduce the odds of a consumer-led slowdown, supporting the view that the economy can handle continued focus on inflation 1 2. But firmer demand can also make it harder to bring inflation down from 3.4%, especially if most households still expect grocery bills to climb 2. The likely policy implication is patience. With unemployment low and wage pressure fading, there's little urgency to ease policy to rescue the labor market 1. With inflation still above where policymakers would like it and consumers regaining confidence, there's also little reason to declare victory 2. On balance, the evidence leans toward Schwab's more confident reading. Cooling wage growth removes a major inflation risk, and consumer data show stabilization rather than strain 1 2. Deloitte's "weak jobs" characterization is a useful warning, though, because a labor market that softens slowly can turn quickly 2. The Fed's room to maneuver is real, but it depends on employment holding near current levels. The data points to watch are whether wage growth keeps cooling without job losses accelerating, and whether consumers' improving spending plans translate into demand that keeps price pressures stubborn. If those trends hold, the Fed can keep its attention on inflation. If the job market weakens, that crossroads will arrive sooner than markets expect.
