results.title: Growth Holds, Risks Widen
highlights: - Longer-term themes are driving cyclical trends. As geopolitical fragmentation continues, most major economies are absorbing higher energy prices and tariffs better than expected. In our baseline, we expect global growth to remain resilient over our six- to 12-month cyclical horizon while inflation moderates. an energy price shock, leading investors to price in higher interest rate expectations. Recent policy actions may bolster the credibility of the Federal Reserve and other central banks, which can help reduce investor uncertainty around the medium-term outlook for yields. Longer-term secular forces are driving the six- to 12-month cyclical outlook. Our June 2026 Secular Outlook, “ Rupture and Resilience,” explored the fraying of traditional trade, security, and financial alliances that we had first highlighted in our 2025 Secular Outlook, “ The Fragmentation Era.” This means geopolitics shape growth and inflation more directly. Energy prices, driven sharply higher by the conflict in the Middle East, have increased headline inflation. That has sparked a shift in monetary policy expectations since the conflict began, with markets pricing in interest rate hikes and pushing bond yields higher. The knock-on effects include higher U.S. mortgage rates and increased debt-service costs for companies and governments, all of which could potentially hamper growth. And yet the global economy has remained resilient, including energy-importing countries and U.S. trading partners that face higher tariffs. The main exception is China, where a prolonged and ongoing housing downturn, weak domestic demand, and abundant existing manufacturing capacity weigh on activity and inflation. The rise in energy costs has had only modest spillovers into core inflation and nominal wage growth. Central banks have remained focused on inflation risks and on keeping inflation expectations well-anchored. The additional monetary tightening expected across developed (DM) and emerging market (EM) economies has been well-communicated and is now largely reflected in market pricing. Our baseline is that the Federal Reserve and other major central banks ultimately won’t need to fully deliver the amount of interest rate hikes currently priced into markets. We therefore expect stable global growth to continue in our baseline while inflation moderates as the energy price shock fades. This relatively benign base case rests partly on the assumption that energy prices decline over time in line with expectations priced into futures markets, but an escalation or resolution of the Iran conflict could potentially swing prices significantly. More fundamentally, the benign outlook relies on three economic buffers: 1. The global AI capex cycle continues without generating cyclical overheating. AI-related demand continues to exceed supply. The largest hyperscalers have shifted from financing the infrastructure buildout through operating cash flow and balance-sheet capacity to debt issuance and off-balance-sheet commitments. AI infrastructure investment is also accelerating globally, even as the U.S. and China remain the leaders. 2. Households and China continue to absorb the global hit from higher energy prices. Strong household balance sheets have allowed consumers to uphold spending by drawing down savings. China has absorbed higher input costs through weaker margins, inventory drawdowns, and domestic demand shifts toward renewable energy sources, limiting the pass-through into global goods prices. 3. An incremental central bank policy approach and AI-related risk appetite help keep financial conditions relatively stable. Wage growth and unit labor cost pressures are moderating, long-term inflation expectations remain anchored, and much of the current inflation pressure reflects energy and other non-labor costs. We expect the Fed under Chair Kevin Warsh to preserve its broad policy framework and 2% inflation target, although changes in Fed communication could generate volatility in front-end rates. Risk 2: The energy supply shock worsens and energy prices exceed market expectations Middle East tensions are disrupting oil flows and depleting inventories, even as U.S. Energy Department reports indicate that flows through the Strait of Hormuz have picked up in recent weeks. El Niño could create additional inflation risks through food, fertilizer, and shipping channels. A more severe or persistent energy shock – in addition to increasing the risk of a central bank policy response – could impose a larger real-income burden on households and businesses, while testing China’s capacity to continue absorbing higher input costs. Compounding supply shocks simultaneously spur inflation and erode demand. This could contribute to tighter global financial conditions – i.e., higher interest rates, stricter lending standards, wider credit spreads, and other factors that broadly tend to hamper growth. More restrictive central bank policy is one potential catalyst. After several years of above-target inflation and supply shocks, central banks may place greater weight on the risk that another temporary shock becomes embedded in inflation expectations. In this scenario, policymakers would deliver more tightening than markets currently price. Financial conditions could also tighten for other reasons. Investors may demand greater compensation across a broad range of assets as uncertainty rises, particularly if confidence in the AI investment cycle weakens while energy prices remain elevated. Higher rates could uncover vulnerabilities and raise the risk of financial market accidents. Higher energy prices, which have pressured global yields higher, are adding to government borrowing costs – at a time when debt-to-GDP ratios are near record highs across most economies and fiscal space is limited. However, sovereign debt remains sustainable across most DM countries, in our view, despite the global rise in yields. The U.K., Italy, and Japan remain vulnerable – and Japan increasingly so given recent policies that add to deficits – but their debt trajectories appear sustainable under current fiscal plans. Our expectation is that fiscal concerns will continue to drive episodic market volatility across global markets. However, investors are getting higher sovereign bond yields than a year ago to help compensate for these risks. Furthermore, if governments do tackle necessary fiscal reforms – the planned U.K. budget tightening is a good example – yields have room to fall. In our 2024 Secular Outlook, “ Yield Advantage,” we explored how the post-pandemic inflation shock and rate-hiking cycle had produced a generational reset higher in bond yields. This year, the conflict in the Middle East sparked a new inflation shock that has lifted yields further. Today’s higher yields may provide income that can help offset price declines to a degree that was not possible in 2022. Still, the path higher has been challenging for investors. - Higher energy prices, and their impact on monetary policy expectations, have been the main driver pushing real yields higher. Both real (inflation-adjusted) and nominal yields have shifted meaningfully higher post-pandemic. The latest yield increase reflects higher energy prices, which have overshadowed broader disinflationary trends and caused markets to price in more expected central bank rate hikes than before. Importantly, real yields, not inflation expectations, have been the primary force driving nominal yields higher in recent months, with 10-year breakeven yields showing inflation expectations remain largely unchanged. A prolonged conflict in the Middle East could eventually substantially tighten global financial conditions through a broader range of asset price changes – not just through higher rates – which could potentially hurt growth particularly for energy-importing countries.

results.title: Trump’s diesel deal opens a new rift with Europe over Ukraine | Russia-Ukraine war News | Al Jazeera
highlights: *Trump calls for Zelenskyy to be replaced, while Russia has claimed it can supply even more diesel to the global market than the quantities agreed with United States President Donald Trump. President Vladimir Putin and Trump spoke on Friday on an agreement expected to bring 300,000 tonnes of diesel to global markets in October, half a million tonnes in November, and a million tonnes in December. But experts are sceptical, and the move has opened a rift between the US and Europe on the Ukraine war. Kostis Stambolis, executive director of the Institute of Energy for South-East Europe (IENE), described the US move as “purely political” and designed to put Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy in a corner. Europe has reacted to the diesel deal by backing Ukraine, whose war funding will be “front and centre” of this week’s European Council summit, European Commission President Ursula Von Der Leyen said on Sunday. Stambolis believes Trump was leveraging European weakness to shift its position on Ukraine. Trump is showing the Europeans “he doesn’t want to deal with Europe and to hell with them … This is opening the rift between the US and the EU further,” said Stambolis. Ukraine says it has destroyed roughly half of Russia’s refining capacity, forcing Moscow to stop exporting lucrative petroleum products which help it to finance its war. It has also bombed Russian tankers carrying crude oil to global markets. Zelenskyy said the strategy was effective, and Trump’s deal, which would suspend sanctions on Russian oil products until April 2027, undermined it. Although Trump announced an energy ceasefire between Russia and Ukraine on Sunday, leading Ukraine to suspend its attacks on refineries, Russian strikes pounded Kyiv’s energy grid and killed 12 people in Dnipropetrovsk. Europe supports Ukraine’s economic strategy against Russia’s war machine, but Trump has blamed it for raising petrol prices at the pump for Americans as he heads into Congressional midterm elections in early November. “[Zelenskyy] wants to make problems for our farmers, our ranchers, with diesel fuel because Russia supplies a large portion of the diesel fuel throughout the world,” Trump told reporters in the White House after Zelenskyy’s reaction. I think it’s time for Ukraine to get a new president,” he Trump has followed a seemingly self-contradictory policy towards Russia. He cut US military aid to Ukraine when he assumed power in January 2025, but agreed to sell Europe weapons to help Ukraine. y in the amazing job” Last month, Trump signed the Lindsey Graham Act, which would allow him to punish countries buying Russian oil. Eleven days later, he reversed policy. According to the US Energy Information Agency (EIA), average US diesel and petrol prices briefly spiked but ultimately changed little on account of the Ukraine war, yet they have risen a great deal on account of the US-Israel war on Iran. US diesel was priced at $4.10 a gallon on the day of Russia’s invasion of Ukraine, February 24, 2022. It had fallen to $3.81 on the eve of Trump’s Gulf war, February 28, 2026. It has since risen by 78 percent, to $6.19 in early October. It is a similar story for US regular unleaded gasoline, priced at $3.48 a gallon before the Russian invasion. It stood at $2.79 before Trump’s Gulf war, but has since risen by half, to $4.15 a gallon. The US government has little room to reduce taxes, which constitute just 11 or 12 percent of retail price, so it can only manipulate prices through supply. “If the market knows that there will be much more diesel in the coming weeks, it factors this into today’s prices and discounts it now,” Stambolis told Al Jazeera. But much more important in bringing down oil prices than the Trump-Putin deal will be an October 2 announcement by the G7 to release 100 million barrels of oil from strategic reserves, he said. A remainder of 80 million barrels from a previous, 400-million-tonne release in March will also be released. “This release will start happening in the next two weeks,” Stambolis said. “The world is 5 million barrels a day short of crude compared to before the Gulf war. It’s a very significant percentage on 100 million. All prices vary on this margin.”

results.title: Trump insists energy ceasefire holds as Ukraine reports new Russian strikes | Russia-Ukraine war News | Al Jazeera
highlights: Trump insists energy ceasefire holds as Ukraine reports new Russian strikes | Russia-Ukraine war | Al Jazeera US president urges Zelenskyy, Putin to end ‘ridiculous war’ and insists the two nations have agreed to stop attacks on energy infrastructure. enskyy urges pressure on Russia as NATO warns against escalation United States President Donald Trump has insisted that Russia and Ukraine have agreed to stop striking each other’s energy infrastructure, as he called on both sides to end the “ridiculous” war. Trump’s comments on Monday came even as Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said Russian forces had struck at least six Ukrainian energy facilities since the US president declared the truce on Sunday. Trump had blindsided Kyiv and its European allies when he announced the purported energy ceasefire on Sunday. The announcement came two days after he temporarily eased US sanctions on Russian diesel, a move that drew outrage in Europe and Ukraine. Zelenskyy said on Monday that Ukraine supported an energy ceasefire and had carried out no attacks on Russian refineries overnight. He said Kyiv was prepared to sign “guarantees to make sure they can be trusted”. But he said it was “increasingly evident” that Moscow “Today alone, the Russians have attacked 6 energy facilities in Ukraine. 33 people were wounded across the country,” Zelenskyy wrote on social media. “This is what happens when Russia sees the prospect of higher revenues for its war machine.” Russia, however, has rejected any pause in fighting, with Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov promising to press ahead with the military campaign. “I do not think he deserves a respite,” he said of Zelenskyy. “I don’t think we’ll be buying into assurances and promises again.” Russia, he added, would continue to pursue the goals of what it calls its “special military operation” in Ukraine. Trump, meanwhile, has portrayed Ukraine, rather than Russia, as the main obstacle to peace. He has said that Putin is more eager on a deal than Zelenskyy, and has called on Ukrainians to vote their president out of office – an unusually harsh turn in a relationship that has been strained since Trump returned to the White House in 2025. The latest announcement, according to our correspondent, appeared to be driven by Trump’s desire to bring down diesel prices before the US midterm elections on November 3. Most polls predict that Republicans will lose control of Congress as voters grow frustrated with rising prices, particularly for petrol. Ukraine’s European allies, meanwhile, voiced scepticism about the energy ceasefire and approved the largest set of European Union sanctions since Russia’s 2022 invasion. The bloc’s foreign ministers added some 1,569 people and businesses to the bloc’s sanctions list to maintain the pressure on Moscow. “Russia will only negotiate seriously under pressure, which is why we are sticking to our sanctions against Russia,” German Chancellor Friedrich Merz said in Berlin.

results.title: October 13 Geopolitics: Infrastructure Trust Crisis — Signal Before Noise
highlights: The October 13 analysis shows that the regional crisis has moved from infrastructure threats to a test of governments' ability to protect assets, maintain economic activity, and implement agreements. Saudi attacks, rising energy transportation costs, Hormuz negotiations, Britain's new allegation against Iran, and Ukraine's unverified ceasefire all highlight credibility and implementation guarantees. Lead: Over the past 24 hours, the regional crisis has moved from threatening vital infrastructure to a stage in which governments' ability to protect citizens, maintain trade flows, and implement diplomatic commitments is being questioned. Continued missile and drone attacks on Saudi Arabia, widespread flight disruptions, rising energy shipping and insurance costs, ongoing disagreements between Iran and the United States over Hormuz, and Britain's new accusation against Iran all indicate growing political and economic costs. In Ukraine, the gap between the announced ceasefire and the actual behavior of the parties has also become the central issue. Today's central signal: The crisis is no longer only about the ability to attack infrastructure; the ability to protect it, manage economic consequences, and transform political promises into enforceable commitments has now become decisive. The October 12 report emphasized the transformation of vital infrastructure into an instrument of political pressure. Developments on October 13 show that this trend has entered a new phase: the cost of defending infrastructure, economic disruption caused by insecurity, and the credibility of warning systems and agreements have become as important as the attacks themselves. In Saudi Arabia, new missile and drone attacks were reported on October 12. At the same time, an investigation into the performance of defense systems and public warnings has begun. In a report published at 23:39 UTC on October 12, Reuters put the death toll from the recent series of attacks on Riyadh airport at at least 18; this figure must be distinguished from the 13 deaths associated with the specific October 10 attack. Reuters In transportation, an aviation notice issued on October 12 indicates that Riyadh airport will remain closed until October 17. Several international airlines have also canceled or suspended flights. Reuters Regarding Iran and the United States, Iran's Foreign Ministry spokesperson announced that Tehran was still reviewing Washington's response to the Hormuz reopening proposal and would respond through intermediaries after completing its review. Therefore, contrary to a possible interpretation of the previous day's statements, it cannot be concluded that indirect communication has completely stopped. Reuters In energy markets, Brent crude ended Monday's trading at $106.65 but declined to approximately $106.04 in early Tuesday trading. Ministers from countries participating in OPEC and non-OPEC cooperation also warned that shipping and insurance costs in some energy flows had reached more than one-third of cargo value. Reuters In Europe, Britain's prime minister accused Iran of possible involvement in a suspected plot against Fairford air base. Iran rejected the allegation. In Ukraine, new attacks on energy infrastructure continued, and the purported ceasefire agreement has not yet become a mechanism confirmed by both sides. Reuters Executive Conclusion: Today's main change is the shift in the crisis's center of gravity from “destructive capability” to “protective capability, continuity of economic activity, and credibility of commitments.” On October 12, Iranian Foreign Ministry spokesperson Esmaeil Baghaei announced that Tehran was reviewing the U.S. response to its proposal concerning the reopening of the Strait of Hormuz. He also confirmed that messages continued to be exchanged through intermediaries. Qatar and Pakistan are among the countries involved in mediation efforts. The main disagreement still concerns the sequence of negotiations: Washington wants to address Iran's nuclear program early, while Tehran emphasizes reopening Hormuz and restoring maritime security as initial subjects. Reuters On October 12, Brent crude closed at $106.65, an increase of $1.93. At the beginning of October 13 trading, its price was approximately $106.04. At the same time, ministers from countries participating in OPEC and non-OPEC cooperation announced that shipping and insurance costs in some energy flows had reached more than one-third of commodity value. On October 12, British Prime Minister Andy Burnham stated that, according to his government's assessment, a suspected plot against RAF Fairford air base was probably coordinated in Iran and almost certainly directed by the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps. On October 12, Ukrainian officials reported Russian attacks on at least six energy-related targets. Zelenskyy announced that Ukraine was prepared to halt attacks on energy facilities reciprocally, but Russia continued attacking. The Kremlin confirmed continuing contacts but did not clearly confirm implementation of the ceasefire announced by Trump. The European Union also added 1,569 new names to its Russia-related sanctions list. Reuters On October 12, Gaza medical authorities reported that an Israeli strike in the southern part of the territory had killed at least two people. The Israeli military stated that the target was a militant. Israel accuses Hamas of violating the ceasefire, while Hamas denies the allegations. This development occurred while the implementation of essential provisions of the October 2025 ceasefire agreement continues to face serious difficulties. Reuters October 13: The ability to protect infrastructure, maintain economic activity, and establish the credibility of agreements became the central issue. First, in Saudi Arabia, the issue has expanded from missile impacts to air-defense performance, public warnings, and the airport's prolonged closure. Second, in Hormuz, the question is not merely reopening the route; insurance costs, safe passage, and agreement implementation guarantees are also decisive. Third, in Ukraine, the political announcement of a ceasefire has not yet become a verifiable cessation of attacks. The new phase can be described as “a crisis of credibility in protection and implementation of commitments.” Signal | Negative Signal | | --- | --- | | Continued Iran–U.S. message exchanges | No 1. The U.S. decision on direct participation in operations against the Houthis. 2. New attacks on Saudi airports and energy facilities. 3. Results of the air-defense investigation and performance of Saudi Arabia's public warning system. 4. Timing and conditions for reopening Riyadh airport. 5. Iran's formal response to the U.S. proposal concerning Hormuz. 6. New mediation steps by Qatar and Pakistan. 7. Changes in war-risk insurance and maritime transportation costs. 8. Oil-price fluctuations and the supply of Russian petroleum products. 9. Possible British measures against Iran and Tehran's response. 10. Signs of actual implementation of the energy ceasefire in Ukraine. 11. New European Union decisions concerning sanctions on Russia. 12. Ceasefire implementation and continued attacks in Gaza. Today's developments show that war and diplomacy have entered a phase in which the credibility of governments and agreements has become as important as military capability. “The main signal of October 13 is that the crisis has shifted from competition over infrastructure destruction to competition over the credibility of protection and implementation of commitments. Unless operational security, public trust, and agreement implementation guarantees are strengthened simultaneously, temporary reductions in attacks or verbal diplomatic progress will not be sufficient to restore stability.”

results.title: Trump Blindsides Ukraine But Gives Europe an Opportunity | Carnegie Endowment for International Peace
highlights: Ahead of a tough winter for Ukraine, Donald Trump’s swing back toward Russia bodes ill. But instead of panicking, Kyiv’s European allies are focusing on action. Less than forty-eight hours after U.S. President Donald Trump announced a waiver for purchases of Russian diesel and a so-called energy ceasefire between Russia and Ukraine, one that was news to Kyiv and ignored by Moscow, the EU approved the largest expansion of its Russia sanctions list since the start of the war. Amid the international reaction, Trump renewed his call for Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky to be replaced. At the same time, at the Warsaw Security Forum, the highest ranking U.S. military official in Europe, the Supreme Allied Commander Europe General Alexus Grynkewich, attempted in a rare speech to reinforce the NATO’s deterrence by laying out his, and the alliance’s, theory of victory against Putin. And by the end of the day, French President Emmanuel Macron published video of his naval forces boarding and searching a ship in the Russian ghost fleet, used to smuggle oil products and circumvent sanctions. European leaders did not go into a public tailspin after decision by a U.S. president that could potentially harm security. With the timeline and applicability of Trump’s decision up in the air of U.S. laws, Europeans stayed their course. It is perhaps a quiet signal of how things are changing in the transatlantic alliance. There was no publicly discernable urgent panic, no careful staging of videoconferences, or announcements of billion-euro acquisitions of U.S. weapons to try to placate Trump and contain the fallout. Ukraine is staring at a very challenging winter ahead, and Russia’s bombing campaign over recent weeks has been ferocious and exacting, especially against the country’s energy and critical infrastructure. Kyiv is facing a critical shortage of American Patriot air defense munitions, which are the most capable system for intercepting Russian ballistic missiles—and the United States, and European firms looking to start production in 2027, cannot build fast enough. But European leaders, including Zelensky, have learned from the many previous rounds of rollercoaster diplomacy with Trump. Their statements welcoming an energy ceasefire are meant to show that they are not obstructing the president’s desire to end this war that has stubbornly withstood his art of the deal. They have also learned that the best way to give themselves cards with the White House, and more importantly in the theater of war, is by accelerating their sanctions, producing more weapons, and increasing their readiness and resilience. More than half of the sanctions the EU agreed at the September 12, 2026, Foreign Affairs Council are connected to the production chain of ballistic missiles, according to the bloc’s top diplomat Kaja Kallas. Sanctions don air defense batteries interceptors, but they can disrupt Russia s ability to produce its own at speed Europeans are working on concretely assisting Ukraine, despite the slowness of their production lines and the limits of their fiscal space, and despite consensus over the seizing of Russian frozen assets continuing to elude them. In mid-September, Germany got U.S. approval to transfer ten of its Patriot batteries to Ukraine, even though the notification to Congress was not accompanied by a concurrent announcement of backfill-replacement missiles being shipped to Germany. France and Italy are meant to deliver Aster 30 missiles by the end of October, 2026, and their own air defense system, the SAMP/T batteries, by 2027. And Europeans have massively stepped up their supply of intelligence and targeting support for Ukraine since the last time the U.S. cut off intelligence sharing. Time is of the essence for Ukraine, as the next three months look to be the hardest when, according to Zelensky, the country has received only about one-third as many anti-aircraft missiles so far this year as it did in 2025. narrow local industrial and hinder transformational leaps Franco-German cooperation a next generation aircraft and tank, as well as their inability to come together on air-defense industrial projects are major setbacks. Division and disunity also cast a shadow. With the EU in the last phases of ending its energy purchases from Russia, while energy prices continue to rise, mainly because of the Iran war, and as constituencies grow more disgruntled, support for resuming those Russian energy purchases could increase in certain European quarters—especially now Trump has broken the taboo. Moreover, the upcoming review of the United States’ force posture in Europe has highlighted the disparate ways various European allies prefer dealing with how America is rethinking its role in the continent’s security. Despite these serious challenges, the past few days have shown that Europeans are maturing as geopolitical actors, even with regard to their historic American protector. In the grand scheme of things, this is a much better state of affairs for the alliance and its longevity.

results.title: Global Growth Holds Near 3% Despite War, Energy and Trade Shocks | Previct.ai
highlights: Autumn forecasts from banks, ministries and central banks have been revised slightly higher, but Nordea warns the resilience rests on fragile geopolitics and costly shipping routes. - Autumn forecasts from banks, ministries, central banks and international organisations broadly converge on global growth of about 3% this year and next, with most revisions slightly higher. - Nordea attributes the resilience partly to heavy investment in artificial intelligence, defence and the green and digital transition, which it expects to increase in coming years, especially in Europe. - The same forecasts flag considerable uncertainty: Middle East and Ukraine conflicts, plus shipping disruption around the Strait of Hormuz and the Red Sea, are already raising freight, energy and commodity costs. The global economy is showing no sign of a significant slowdown despite the war in the Middle East, higher energy prices, continued trade tensions and tighter financial conditions, according to Nordea's macro view. Growth expectations have been revised slightly upward in most autumn forecasts now being published by banks, ministries, central banks and international organisations, with broad agreement that global growth will run around 3% this year and next — close to trend. Nordea's assessment credits much of the resilience to large-scale investment in artificial intelligence, the defence industry and the green and digital transition. Those spending programmes are expected to grow further in the coming years, not least in Europe, giving the expansion a source of demand that is less sensitive to the geopolitical headlines weighing on sentiment. The bank's view is that this investment offset, combined with still-tight financial conditions, has kept the global economy from tipping into a meaningful downturn. The same forecasters agree that considerable uncertainty surrounds that outcome, and Nordea points to a fragile geopolitical backdrop as the main reason. The conflicts in the Middle East and Ukraine weigh most heavily, but the bank also cites China's ambitions regarding Taiwan, Argentina's renewed claim to the Falkland Islands and the recently resolved situation around Greenland as evidence that geopolitics now shapes the economic outlook differently than it has for many years. Those risks are already transmitting into costs. Nordea notes that a blockade of the Strait of Hormuz and military actions targeting shipping in the Red Sea and oil facilities in affected countries show up immediately as longer delivery times, rising freight rates and significantly higher energy and commodity prices. That combination raises cost pressure on businesses and hits households directly. Europe's summer drought adds further pressure on consumer prices, compounding the energy and shipping channel. The practical read is that the roughly 3% growth consensus is a baseline, not a guarantee. It holds only while the investment drivers — AI, defence and the green and digital transition — keep expanding and the geopolitical shocks stay contained to cost channels rather than escalating into outright supply disruption. A widening of the Middle East conflict or a sustained closure of key shipping routes would work through freight, energy and commodity prices into business costs and household budgets, the same mechanism Nordea identifies as already active, and would test whether the forecast upgrades can survive.

results.title: EU cautious over Trump’s ‘energy ceasefire’ as Russia continues Ukraine attacks - RFI
highlights: The European Union has given a cautious welcome to the prospect of an “energy ceasefire” between Russia and Ukraine, as winter approaches and renewed Russian strikes put fresh pressure on the country’s power network. EU foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas struck a cautious note on Monday, saying Brussels wanted to see clear evidence that Moscow intended to respect the proposed halt to attacks on energy infrastructure announced by US President Donald Trump. Those doubts deepened through the day as Ukraine said Russia had continued to strike energy sites, while the Kremlin stopped short of confirming that any ceasefire had been agreed. The dispute comes amid wider unease among Ukraine’s European allies after Trump announced at the weekend a temporary easing of US sanctions on Russian diesel – a move Kyiv and several European governments fear could reduce pressure on President Vladimir Putin to end the war. Trump defended the diesel deal on Monday despite criticism from US . He also Russia and Ukraine had agreed to an energy ceasefire reporters: “ I said they agreed.” Trump sowed confusion on Sunday when he announced an “ energy ceasefire” between Russia and Ukraine without setting out its terms or explaining how it would be enforced. But Russia continued attacking Ukraine’s power infrastructure. Zelensky said at least six energy targets were hit on Monday, including a gas facility and a petrol station, after earlier strikes on power plants in Kyiv and Kharkiv. Russia said contacts were continuing over a possible energy ceasefire, but Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov rejected Kyiv’s call for a broader pause. With colder weather approaching, attacks on the electricity network remain a central concern after successive winters in which Russia has targeted Ukrainian energy infrastructure. Kallas warned that any agreement would also need to go beyond oil refineries, arguing that a narrowly defined truce would favour Moscow because Russia has far greater refining capacity. The limits of Russia’s willingness to halt military operations were underlined when the Kremlin rejected Zelensky’s proposal for a 60-day ceasefire that would allow Ukraine to organise and campaign for a presidential election. Peskov said Putin would instead be prepared to order Russian forces not to strike Ukraine on election day itself. “If they truly want to hold elections in Kyiv, then the president of Russia, the commander-in-chief, will be ready to give an order not to launch strikes on Ukraine on election day, specifically on election day,” he said. The offer fell well short of Kyiv’s call for the security conditions needed to organise voting while millions of Ukrainians remain displaced at home and abroad. The tougher message was also on display at the Warsaw Security Forum, where NATO’s top military commander warned that any attack on an alliance member would be made “utterly futile”. US General Alexus Grynkewich, NATO’s Supreme Allied Commander Europe, said the alliance was ready to “block, blunt and break” an assault. European governments are also focused on cyberattacks, sabotage and disinformation attributed to Russia. Lithuanian Prime Minister Mindaugas Sinkevicius told the forum that Ukraine’s allies should encourage Kyiv to strike more Russian data centres as part of efforts to counter Moscow’s hybrid warfare capabilities. Three attacks have been reported against data centres belonging to Yandex, Russia’s biggest technology company. Zelensky said Russian bot activity appeared to have declined following the attacks, although their impact has not been independently verified. For the EU, the immediate test remains whether Trump’s proposed energy ceasefire translates into an actual pause in attacks as another winter approaches. on hybrid car exports

results.title: Geopolitical conflict and its impact on global markets
highlights: - Iran conflict and oil prices: Restricted Strait of Hormuz shipping keeps global oil, natural gas, freight and inflation risks in focus. - Geopolitical risks and global markets: The Russia-Ukraine war and Middle East conflict continue to influence trade, energy flows and investor confidence. - Geopolitical market volatility: Diversification and a long-term plan can help investors respond to conflict-driven market swings without overreacting to headlines. The Iran conflict and Russia-Ukraine war continue to shape global markets through oil prices, shipping routes, trade policy and inflation expectations. The most immediate risk runs through the Strait of Hormuz, a narrow waterway used to move large volumes of oil and liquefied natural gas. Investors should focus less on each headline and more on whether these conflicts cause lasting supply losses that change economic growth, inflation or corporate profits. Iran moved to the center of investor attention after U.S. and Israeli military operations expanded in late February. A ceasefire announced in April briefly supported renewed tanker traffic, but later attacks and restrictions have kept Strait of Hormuz shipping well below normal. When fighting began, the S&P 500 fell 9% from its January peak, while developed international and emerging market stocks declined 8% to 12%, before markets rebounded and reached new all-time highs as investors refocused on consumer spending, corporate earnings and changing Gulf energy flows. 1 International markets face greater potential pressure because many European and Asian economies import a larger share of the energy they consume. The United States produces more of its own energy, but higher global prices still raise costs for American households and businesses. Recent market resilience does not eliminate geopolitical risk; it shows that investors continue to weigh conflict against the economy’s ability to absorb disruption. and global markets because few routes can replace the Strait of Hormuz at similar scale. The U.S. Energy Information Administration estimates that about 20 million barrels of oil per day moved through the strait in 2024, equal to roughly 20% of global petroleum liquids consumption. About 20% of global liquefied natural gas trade also used this route, leaving major importers in Europe and Asia especially sensitive to slower traffic. 2 Sources: U.S. Bank Asset Management Group Research, U.S. Energy Information Administration via FRED (Crude Oil Price: West Texas Intermediate – Cushing, Oklahoma, Dollars per Barrel), Federal Reserve Bank of St. Louis and Bloomberg. As of August 4, 2026. The International Energy Agency describes the Strait of Hormuz as a pivotal bottleneck for oil shipped by sea. The threat of slower traffic can lift prices before a physical shortage develops because energy markets quickly account for tighter supply, longer routes and higher shipping costs. If those increases persist, they can raise transportation and production expenses, strain household budgets and reduce corporate profit margins. Current conditions fit a “disrupted but absorbing” scenario. Shipping remains constrained, including along the Bab el-Mandeb route near the Red Sea, while inventories, reserve releases, added production, alternate routes and demand reductions continue to cushion the loss of supply. China in particular reduced crude oil imports this year, mitigating some demand pressure. Oil prices remain elevated but contained because these adjustments have limited the gap between available supply and demand. The Russia-Ukraine war remains an important backdrop for global markets more than four years after Russia invaded Ukraine. The conflict continues to influence trade policy, energy flows and economic sanctions, which governments use to limit financial activity and commerce. Markets have adapted to recurring developments, but changes in fighting, negotiations or sanctions can still influence business decisions, government spending and investor confidence. Oil prices surged after Russia’s 2022 invasion as Western governments imposed sanctions on a major energy exporter. The initial spike faded as buyers found new suppliers, trade routes shifted and markets gained a clearer view of available supply. 4 Recent Ukraine strikes on Russian oil and refining infrastructure could add pressure to global energy costs if Strait of Hormuz shipping remains constrained. “Investors are navigating a lot of moving parts in 2026, adding geopolitical conflict to a change in Federal Reserve leadership and midterm elections,” says Terry Sandven, chief equity strategist with U.S. Bank Asset Management Group. “ Inflation is kryptonite to stock valuations. If energy prices rise and prices for other goods follow, higher borrowing costs could temper corporate earnings.” His comments highlight the risk that a prolonged energy shock could spread to broader inflation, interest rates and company profits. The U.S. military operation in Venezuela in early January generated dramatic headlines but limited market disruption. Investors treated the event as contained because it did not immediately threaten global energy supplies. The episode illustrates why the scale, duration and economic reach of a conflict often influence markets more than the initial surprise. Geopolitical tensions can also influence markets without military conflict. New trade barriers, sanctions or alliances can alter supply chains, currency values and business investment. Investors can better distinguish temporary volatility from a lasting market risk by asking whether a development changes inflation, growth or corporate earnings. Recent conflicts show that stock prices can recover after investors assess the likely economic impact, while oil prices can retreat after an initial surge if enough supply remains available. Steady economic data, resilient consumer spending and corporate earnings growth have helped support U.S. stock markets during periods of geopolitical volatility. Those fundamentals can absorb a temporary shock, although a prolonged energy disruption could weaken them over time. Geopolitics refer to events that influence the global landscape, including political or trade tensions and military conflicts. Such events often create economic uncertainty, which can lead to fluctuations in stock prices, interest rates, and currencies. Geopolitical conflicts frequently impact supply chains, such as Iran’s threats to halt oil shipments through the Strait of Hormuz. Wars in agricultural regions can also affect crop yields and deliveries. Events like these can cause supply-demand disruptions, resulting in higher prices. The emergence of new geopolitical conflicts often causes an immediate market reaction, frequently a negative one. If events are seen as disruptive to the global economy, investors may suddenly reduce portfolio risk and pursue a so-called “flight to quality.” This approach often results in a sell-off in stocks, with increased interest in bonds or “safe haven” assets like gold. Oil prices can move quickly when investors fear disruption to shipping routes near major producers, even before supply is physically interrupted. When energy prices rise, markets may worry about higher inflation and slower growth, which can pressure stock prices in the short run. The impact often depends on whether higher prices persist long enough to influence household budgets and business costs. The Russia-Ukraine war remains a persistent source of uncertainty because it intersects with trade policy, energy flows, and economic sanctions. Markets have adjusted to the ongoing conflict, but changes in sanctions, negotiations, or energy conditions can still influence prices and confidence. Investors often focus on whether developments change real economic activity or remain primarily a source of headline-driven volatility.

results.title: Europe Pushes Back Against Trump’s Russian Diesel Deal, Vows to Keep Sanctions
highlights: In brief: European governments have criticized US President Donald Trump’s Russian diesel agreement and pledged to maintain pressure on Moscow. Their initial responses combine opposition to sanctions relief with calls to preserve US cooperation and secure a reciprocal halt to attacks on energy infrastructure. by Lesia Dubenko | Oct. 13, 2026, 1:10 pm European governments have pushed back against US President Donald Trump’s diesel agreement with Russia, pledging to maintain sanctions as Germany opposed following Washington’s lead and EU ministers warned against rewarding Moscow while its attacks on Ukraine continue. The clearest responses emerged on Oct. 12, three days after Trump announced the arrangement with Russian leader Vladimir Putin. The EU also approved its largest single expansion of sanctions listings against Russia’s military-industrial complex, underscoring the divergence between Brussels and Washington. Trump presented the diesel deal as a way to ease fuel prices. As Kyiv Post reported, the arrangement envisages Russian supplies to US and global markets, backed by a temporary US sanctions authorization through April 2027. European officials instead emphasized the risk of giving Russia economic relief before it changes its conduct in Ukraine. German Chancellor Friedrich Merz said Berlin would maintain sanctions and argued that Russia’s continued attacks justified stronger restrictions. Merz said pressure was necessary to bring Moscow to the table for serious negotiations. He pointed to Russian strikes on civilian energy infrastructure following Trump’s announcement of an energy ceasefire over the weekend. The chancellor nevertheless said European governments remained in contact with Washington on a common approach to ending the war, acknowledging disagreements over strategy. At the EU foreign ministers’ meeting in Luxembourg, Ireland’s Helen McEntee described the diesel agreement as concerning and urged renewed pressure on Russia, while stressing that cooperation with the US remained essential. She called on European countries to increase support for Ukraine, including through the use of frozen Russian assets. Lithuania’s Kęstutis Budrys argued that the arrangement would help neither fuel prices nor transatlantic unity. Estonia’s Margus Tsahkna linked it to US domestic politics ahead of November’s midterm elections and questioned its practical impact. On Oct. 12, the European Council adopted sanctions against 1,569 individuals and entities, comprising 826 Russian companies and 743 executives. The council attributed the measures to Russia’s escalating aggression and attacks on civilian infrastructure. The decision followed earlier council calls for increased pressure, rather than being presented as a package devised in response to Trump’s announcement. European ministers supported a halt to attacks on energy infrastructure only if Russia also complied, according to the council’s account of the meeting. She also warned that an arrangement focused solely on refineries would disproportionately benefit Russia, whose refining network is much larger than Ukraine’s. Zelensky said Russian attacks on Ukraine’s electricity infrastructure continued after Trump’s Oct. 11 announcement, while Kyiv had temporarily refrained from strikes on Russian energy facilities. Trump defended the agreement on Oct. 12, despite continued Russian attacks after his announcement that an energy ceasefire had taken effect. A day earlier, Trump had declared that both Ukraine and Russia had agreed to stop attacks on energy infrastructure immediately. His announcement caught Zelensky by surprise: The Ukrainian president said Kyiv was still awaiting details from Washington. By Oct. 12, the Kremlin had still not confirmed an agreement. Kremlin spokesperson Dmitry Peskov said contacts were continuing, while Zelensky said Ukraine had temporarily held off striking Russian energy facilities, but Moscow continued attacking Ukraine’s power grid. The diesel concession also came before the first major deadline under the sanctions legislation Trump signed on Sept. 18. Graham sanctions law explains, Oct. Iran Act of 26. The law targets financial institutions, foreign military suppliers and shipping networks, substantial discretion through waivers and tariff Signing the law does not itself establish how much additional pressure Moscow will face. With that deadline still five days away, Washington has already granted relief for Russian diesel, while the scale of its implementation of the new penalties remains to be seen. The dispute comes after Ukrainian attacks forced major Russian refineries to reduce production, with effects visible in both plant operations and export figures. Reuters reported on Sept. 15 that three of Russia’s six largest diesel-producing refineries had significantly reduced or halted output following drone strikes. Kirishi was shut, while Volgograd and NORSI were operating at roughly a quarter of their designed capacity, according to market sources. Together, the six plants normally account for about half of Russian diesel production. September’s seaborne diesel and gasoil shipments subsequently fell 28% from August to 144,000 barrels a day, their lowest level in more than a decade of Vortexa records, That decline, however, reflects both refinery damage and Moscow’s restrictions on exports to preserve domestic supplies. It does not represent an equivalent collapse in all Russian petroleum exports: higher fuel oil and naphtha shipments pushed total seaborne oil-product exports to a three-month high. Nonetheless, Russia is now promising a recovery. Deputy Prime Minister Alexander Novak said on Oct. 12 that diesel exports could return to 3 million to 3.5 million metric tons a month by year-end, as Reuters reported. That remains a forecast, with deliveries dependent on available fuel and the recovery of a refining network Ukraine has repeatedly struck.

highlights: Geopolitical risk has always been priced into investment decisions, but rarely has it demanded a rethink of the assumptions beneath them. Today it does. The question facing long-term investors is no longer whether geopolitical events move markets. It is whether the frameworks built over decades to guide portfolio construction, exclusion policy, and asset allocation still hold in a world that is becoming less rules-based, more fragmented, and harder to model. The conventional wisdom on geopolitical risk has long been reassuring; however dramatic the headlines, asset prices tend to absorb the shock and move on. But as Marcus Svedberg, Chief Economist at Folksam, notes, that view comes with an important condition: “Asset prices don’t tend to be long-term impacted by geopolitical events. But if the geopolitical event impacts commodities, then it may be different.” Svedberg points to the Strait of Hormuz as a case in point, with over 20% of global oil and gas passing through it, any disruption feeds directly into inflation, reprices interest rate expectations, and leaves a mark on bond markets that equity indices, still buoyed by strong corporate earnings, have yet to fully reflect. What makes today’s environment structurally different goes beyond energy markets. Country risk, sovereign bond exposure, and cross-asset correlations are all being re-examined. The rules-based order that reinforced those frameworks for decades is eroding, and the investment industry is only beginning to work out what replaces it. The vocabulary shift is telling, as Kristofer Dreiman, Chief Sustainability Officer at Länsförsäkringar, observes, “We have almost exchanged the words ESG and sustainability for resilience, independence, and sovereignty in the last 24 months.” It reflects a genuine recalibration of what investors consider material risk. Nowhere is that recalibration more visible than in the debate around defense. Nordic investors, historically among the strictest in applying exclusions to the weapons sector, are revisiting policies that in some cases date back over a decade. Yet the shift is not unconditional; sensitivity towards involvement in conflict and potential human rights violations remains high, and beneficiary expectations continue to set real limits on how far the defense pivot can go. Meanwhile, the broader question of how to handle norm violations is becoming more demanding; the caseload is expanding, the analytical work is harder, and the principle of engaging before excluding is under growing pressure. As the number of conflicts grows and investment policies become more nuanced, the demand for reliable, granular data has moved from useful to essential. Deciding whether a company is involved in a norm violation, whether linked to human rights, labor rights, or operations in conflict-affected areas, is not a mechanical exercise. It requires triangulating multiple sources: data providers, company disclosures, and independent authorities such as NGOs or public investigations. When those sources align, the path forward is clearer. results.title: Iran fortifies nuclear sites, prepares for renewed war: report
highlights: Iran is fortifying nuclear sites and threatening wider regional retaliation as it prepares for possible renewed US strikes after November's midterm elections. Iran is strengthening its nuclear and military facilities, mobilising supporters and threatening a wider regional conflict as it prepares for the possibility of renewed war with the United States, according to a report by *The Wall Street Journal.* Iranian leaders believe US President Donald Trump could launch fresh attacks after the 3 November midterm elections, prompting Tehran to reinforce sensitive sites and warn Washington that another offensive would trigger a more devastating response, the newspaper reported on Tuesday. Citing Iranian officials and people familiar with regional communications, the *WSJ* said Tehran had issued both public and private warnings that renewed US strikes could lead to attacks on American interests and Gulf allies. Satellite imagery has shown Iran strengthening defences around nuclear facilities and border areas, while authorities have stepped up pro-government rallies and promoted military training for civilians. Iran's limited ability to counter advanced US fighter jets, high-altitude bombers and cruise missiles has pushed Tehran to rely increasingly on threats of wider retaliation to deter Washington, according to the report. Iranian officials have raised the possibility of launching ground incursions into neighbouring countries in response to further US attacks, according to people familiar with Tehran's warnings. Senior Iranian national security official Mohsen Rezaei warned on Sunday that the United Arab Emirates could be targeted, along with regional data centres and internet cables. Tehran has also warned Arab officials that critical infrastructure, including Saudi oil facilities, could come under attack if fighting resumes, the *WSJ* reported. Iran has also told intermediaries that it could respond more forcefully against American military personnel, including by attempting to sink US warships and inflict casualties among their crews. The warnings highlight the risks to the Gulf's vital economic infrastructure if Trump orders another round of strikes. The US military is also preparing for a possible resumption of hostilities, with a third aircraft carrier strike group and an additional Marine unit heading towards the region according to the outlet. The Pentagon is considering sending more air defence systems and ammunition to American bases across the region. Trump ruled out launching an attack before the midterm elections last week but publicly raised the possibility of striking Iran's Mount Pickaxe nuclear site. US officials said the military was developing several options for renewed strikes. Direct fighting between Washington and Tehran has eased considerably since late July, when Trump backed away from plans for a major escalation, partly over concerns about dwindling interceptor missile stocks needed to protect American and regional targets. Iran has used the period to rebuild missile and drone production facilities and replenish its weapons stockpiles, while Washington has intensified economic pressure on Tehran. Meanwhile, attacks on commercial shipping and tankers in the Gulf and Strait of Hormuz have increased. At least three merchant vessels came under attack over the weekend, according to the United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations agency. A drone strike on the Emirati tanker Petro Dolphin near Oman on Sunday sparked a fire aboard the vessel and left two Indian sailors missing. Satellite images taken by Vantor and analysed by the Washington-based Institute for Science and International Security show Iran constructing new defensive barriers around its Pickaxe Mountain and Natanz nuclear facilities. Behnam Ben Taleblu, senior director of the Iran programme at the Washington-based Foundation for Defense of Democracies, said Tehran's political rhetoric and military preparations indicated it was actively preparing for another confrontation. He described the measures as serving both deterrence and war planning.

results.title: Trump faces a new crisis with Kyiv after the agreement on Russian diesel
highlights: Trump faces a new crisis with Kyiv after the agreement on Russian diesel Ukrainians and Europeans receive with bewilderment the decision of the USA to suspend the sanctions on Putin's fuel Trump's new diplomatic crisis over Ukraine erupted on Friday at Steve Witkoff's exclusive golf club, Shell Bay, on the outskirts of Miami. Senior Ukrainian and European officials had traveled there to hold talks with Trump's peace envoys, Witkoff and Jared Kushner, the president's son-in-law. They planned to discuss updated proposals to end the war in Ukraine before a new trip to Russia. But both soon made an announcement that left their interlocutors and much of the world stunned. The Americans communicated that the United States would suspend sanctions on Russian diesel. They also conveyed a firm request from Trump: that Ukraine stop attacking Russian oil refineries. Now the dispute has become the most serious crisis between Washington and Kyiv since the outbreak of tension in the Oval Office with the Ukrainian president last year. The future of US support for Ukraine is once again at stake. The escalation of recriminations has highlighted how Trump's efforts to lower energy prices before next month's midterm legislative elections threaten to destabilize the fragile negotiations over Ukraine. For Ukrainians and their European allies, attacks on Russian refineries are Kyiv's most effective way of responding to Russian bombings against Ukraine's energy grid. Zelensky has stated that he is willing to stop attacking energy infrastructure if Russia does the same. But Russia has refused. Despite this, Trump considers the Ukrainian attacks an offense against an administration that has continued to provide intelligence and some military support to Ukraine, despite the harsh statements by the American president against Zelensky. Diesel prices, in particular, have become a headache for Trump, because they increase the costs for farmers just as the harvest season begins and there are only a few weeks left until the midterm elections. "He better stop once and for all," Trump told reporters on Saturday, referring to Zelensky and the Ukrainian attacks against Russian refineries, ignoring the Russian bombings against the Ukrainian energy grid. "He wants to create problems for the world. He wants to create problems for our farmers and ranchers." Export statistics indicate that the rise in diesel and energy prices is mainly due to Trump's war against Iran, although the Ukrainian attacks against Russia have contributed to it. On Sunday, Trump claimed on social media that Russia and Ukraine had agreed to an "energy ceasefire" with immediate effect. Neither side confirmed the agreement. "They agreed to it because I said they agreed to it," Trump stated on Monday at the White House. He also reiterated his frustration with Zelensky. "I think Putin is more eager to reach an agreement than Zelensky," said the president. On Monday, European and Ukrainian leaders suggested they would be willing to accept an energy truce, but expressed doubts about whether Russia would respect it. Ukrainian Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha noted that Moscow had attacked Ukrainian energy infrastructure on Sunday night, "a few hours after" the announcement. But the agreement between Trump and Putin regarding diesel quickly overshadowed the rest of the conversations. On Friday, Zelenskyy described the agreement to allow imports of Russian diesel to lower prices as a "weak decision." As the dispute intensified, Trump stated on Saturday that Ukraine needed "a new president." Several European leaders, including French President Emmanuel Macron and European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen, publicly expressed their support for Zelenskyy. Members of the U.S. Congress criticized the diesel deal because, according to them, it helps fund the Russian war machine. "The United States should not provide Putin with a financial lifeline while Russia continues to kill Ukrainian civilians," a bipartisan group of six senators, including Republicans Susan Collins of Maine and John Curtis of Utah, said in a statement on Sunday. "The administration must rectify this immediately." Seibert, a senior EU who attended Friday's meeting in Florida, briefed the ambassadors of 7 member states on the meeting on Sunday main conclusions of meeting in Florida, Seibert explained to them that the Americans were maintaining more contacts with Russians than they were publicly acknowledging. The Trump administration argues that the agreements with Putin, in addition to contributing to lower energy prices, would facilitate an agreement in Ukraine because they would demonstrate to Russia that it can return to the global economy if it agrees to make concessions in the conflict.

results.title: 2026 Is Proving To Be A Defining Year In Geopolitics
highlights: 2026 is turning out as a defining year in geopolitics, but for whom? Opinion 26.08.2026 The US–Israeli war with Iran has proved more consequential for global energy security, trade and international stability than initially anticipated, while the US military intervention in Venezuela challenged established principles of national sovereignty and international law. Geopolitics: Not since the wars in Afghanistan and Iraq reshaped global security after 2001 or, more significantly, since the fall of the Berlin Wall in 1989 and the dissolution of the Soviet Union in 1991, has the international order undergone change on the scale we are witnessing today. The US–Israeli war with Iran has proved more consequential for global energy security, trade and international stability than initially anticipated, while the US military intervention in Venezuela challenged established principles of national sovereignty and international law. Beyond the headlines, however, the transatlantic alliance is under its greatest strain in decades, divided over Iran, Ukraine, trade, defence spending and the reliability of American security guarantees. America’s tariffs, export controls and industrial subsidies have turned trade into an instrument of state power. China, meanwhile, is intensifying military pressure on Taiwan, whose semiconductor industry lies at the heart of global electronics and artificial intelligence. Prof. Barend Prinsloo, director of the Centre for Geopolitical Security and Strategy (CGSS) at the North-West University (NWU), explains that these seismic shifts are being driven by an undercurrent of intensifying competition for control over the currencies, energy resources, technologies and strategic minerals that will determine the global balance of power. dollar remains dominant financial order is “The US dollar has remained the world’s leading reserve and trading currency in 2026, despite continued efforts by BRICS+ countries to reduce their dependence on it. What has changed is not the immediate position of the dollar, but the willingness of countries to explore alternatives. Central banks have accumulated more gold, certain states have expanded trade in their own currencies, and alternative payment mechanisms have received greater attention. We are not witnessing the sudden end of dollar dominance, but the gradual development of a more fragmented international financial system.” Energy security has become a central geopolitical concern “During 2026, energy security has moved to the centre of international competition. Governments are no longer discussing energy only in terms of climate change or economic development; they are treating reliable and affordable energy as a matter of national security. Countries must balance environmental commitments with the immediate need to power industries, protect their economies and reduce their dependence on potentially hostile suppliers. This has simultaneously strengthened the strategic importance of fossil fuels, nuclear power, renewable energy, storage capacity and electricity infrastructure.” into a source “The rapid expansion of artificial intelligence has demonstrated that technological leadership ultimately depends on physical infrastructure. AI requires enormous data centres, advanced semiconductor facilities, extensive cooling systems and, above all, reliable electricity. In 2026, grid capacity has increasingly become a constraint on technological ambition. The global AI race has therefore developed into an energy race as well. Countries capable of expanding their generation and transmission capacity will have an advantage, while those with unreliable electricity systems risk being left behind, regardless of their scientific talent.” “The transatlantic relationship has undergone a fundamental recalibration in 2026. Europe has increased defence spending and accelerated efforts to strengthen its military-industrial capacity because it can no longer assume that the United States will always carry the principal burden of European security. However, Europe remains dependent on American intelligence, logistics, advanced weapons and nuclear deterrence. What has emerged is not complete European strategic autonomy, but the beginning of a long and costly attempt to become less vulnerable to changes in American policy.” , China and Iran remain “Attempts to weaken the relationships among Russia, China and Iran have not produced a decisive realignment in 2026. These countries do not agree on every issue and should not be regarded as a perfectly unified alliance, but they share an interest in limiting American influence and reducing their vulnerability to Western sanctions. Russia’s economic dependence on China, Iran’s integration into BRICS and other alternative institutions, and their shared opposition to Western pressure give them strong reasons to continue cooperating. Their alignment has proved more durable than many Western policymakers may have anticipated.” Globalisation has become increasingly weaponised “Globalisation has not ended in 2026, but its character has changed significantly. Governments continue to depend on international trade, technology and investment, while simultaneously using tariffs, sanctions, export controls, industrial subsidies and access to strategic resources as instruments of national power. Economic interdependence, once presented as a path towards cooperation, has increasingly become a source of vulnerability and leverage. The emerging system is therefore not one of complete deglobalisation, but of weaponised globalisation, in which states carefully distinguish between dependencies they consider beneficial and those they regard as threats.”

results.title: Energy ceasefire: the US threatens Ukraine's weapons supply over refinery strikes | The Macro Notebook
highlights: Trump declared an energy ceasefire as US officials threatened to cut Ukraine's arms and intelligence unless it stops striking Russian refineries, the FT says. The United States has threatened to cut off the system that supplies Ukraine with American weapons unless Kyiv stops striking Russian oil refineries, the Financial Times reported on Sunday, citing officials in Europe, on the day Donald Trump declared an energy ceasefire. The message included threats to end intelligence sharing and the Prioritised Ukraine Requirements List, or Purl, the mechanism through which Ukraine’s allies buy US weapons for it, according to Reuters. US officials were lobbying European capitals as well as Kyiv. “They are calling everyone,” one official told the newspaper. Reuters could not verify the report, and the White House did not comment. Neither side had confirmed the truce. “Effective immediately, there is an ENERGY CEASEFIRE in the War between Russia and Ukraine. Both parties have agreed. Do not break it!” Trump wrote on Truth Social. Volodymyr Zelensky told Axios that the ceasefire “was news for me”, CBS News reported. The Kremlin said only that “contacts are ongoing”, and Ukrainian officials said Russia struck an energy site near Kharkiv in the hours after the post, according to NBC News. The White House wants the refinery strikes stopped because of fuel prices, three weeks before the midterm elections. Trump has blamed Kyiv for high diesel prices in the US, and on Saturday he said Ukraine should get “a new leader who can make a deal”. The prices are real. The average US retail price of diesel was $6.199 a gallon on 5 October, the Energy Information Administration’s weekly survey shows. That is 63% above the $3.809 of 23 February, the month the US went to war with Iran. It peaked at a record $6.529 on 21 September and has fallen 33 cents since. The next figures are due on 14 October. Zelensky put the blame elsewhere. It is easy to link prices with Ukraine, he told ABC News, “when everybody in the world understands” that the war in the Middle East is pushing them up. On Friday the US licensed imports of Russian diesel, which Trump says will start with 300,000 tonnes, followed by 500,000 tonnes in November and more later. As we reported on 12 October, the first cargo covers about 14 hours of US use. The strikes are part of a war that has moved into the air. The two armies are largely deadlocked on the front line, more than four and a half years after the full-scale invasion, and Russia and Ukraine now fight a long-range war of drones and missiles, CBS noted. Shortly before Trump’s post, Zelensky had vowed to keep striking Russian refineries. The campaign is not limited to oil. On Sunday a Ukrainian drone attack shut a data centre run by Yandex in the city of Vladimir, east of Moscow, the third strike on the company’s sites in four days, CBS reported. Outages spread to taxi and banking services in dozens of Russian cities. Zelensky has offered a trade. “We are ready for energy ceasefire, not to attack energy — both sides,” he told ABC. In other words, Ukraine would stop hitting Russian refineries if Russia stopped hitting Ukraine’s power plants. Trump made a similar announcement a month ago, NBC noted, and both sides kept attacking. Europe’s governments are being asked to choose between Washington and Kyiv. Andy Burnham, the British prime minister, backed a mutual halt. “Ukraine is ready if Russia stops its attacks,” he wrote. “This is the best route to get energy and fuel back into world markets.” Mark Carney, Canada’s prime minister, also supported an energy ceasefire but denounced the US deal on Russian diesel, saying it undermined efforts to end the war. Opposition is growing in Washington too. Six US senators, four Republicans and two Democrats, called on the administration to “immediately reverse course” on buying Russian diesel. They said it had not consulted Congress or explained its decision, as the law requires. The threat reaches Europe because Purl is the channel through which allies’ money buys American weapons for Ukraine. Closing it would hit the governments that pay as well as the army that receives. Moscow has not confirmed the ceasefire, and Ukraine says Russian strikes on its energy sites have not stopped. The next Ukrainian strike on a Russian refinery will show whether Kyiv has accepted the American terms. The International Energy Agency’s governing board meets on 15 October to discuss releasing more diesel from emergency stocks, which we cover in a separate item today. The EIA’s weekly survey on 14 October will show whether US diesel prices are still falling.

In this context, economic opportunities may certainly emerge, as illustrated by the current strengthening of trade relations between Saudi Arabia and Brazil, and between the United Arab Emirates and India. But, more broadly, this intensification of rivalries is above all a source of uncertainty, both for governments and economic actors. "Companies have realised that risk, particularly geopolitical risk, is the 'new normal'," warns Tania Sollogoub, who believes that one of the main challenges facing the market today is identifying the channels through which sensitive events are transmitted. "What is striking is the desire of companies to decouple themselves from geopolitical risk and do everything possible to maintain their business, up to a certain point," says Thomas Gomart. But what point? " To set this threshold, many have moved from a binary approach to risk – I accept it or I don't – to a more "realistic" approach. This is characterised by the development of a variety of scenarios, each with its own associated action plans. "We are entering the era of realgeopolitik," sums up Tania Sollogoub, who also sees the possibility of companies becoming misaligned with their own governments as one of the other major dangers of this new era. An era in which the Old Continent does not seem to be entering from a position of strength. Indeed, having lost one of its few comparative advantages – stability – with the outbreak of war in Ukraine, it is currently weakened both by the marked political fragmentation among its member states and the recent fracturing of the transatlantic alliance Thomas Gomart points out, however, that an economically open world requires the major powers to respect a minimum set of rules and believes that, in this respect, "Europe probably has some political room for manoeuvre". Caught between the United States and China, it will nevertheless have its work cut out to make its voice heard and defend its interests. at Rhodium Group. Vance and Secretary of State Marco Rubio, appears more transparent. "The administration's strategy is based on a total withdrawal of the US presence in the world and the formation of a bloc of allies, including Europe, against China," says Andrew Bishop. Paris, Berlin, Madrid, London Recent or upcoming visits by European heads of state and government to China are on the rise. With the transatlantic alliance under strain from the Trump administration, between substantial increases in customs duties and repeated criticism of the Old Continent, the prospect of a rapprochement with the Beijing regime may seem appealing. This is all the more true given that the two powers share certain major challenges and priorities, such as "demographic ageing and the energy transition to a low-carbon model", notes Thomas Gomart, director at IFRI. However, as some experts argue, it is far from certain that the cost/benefit balance of such a move would tip in Europe's favour. "China has little to offer," says Agatha Kratz, a partner at Rhodium Group, who believes that the risks far outweigh the opportunities. The specialist points to: sluggish Chinese economic growth, well below that reflected in official statistics; less promising trade prospects, as evidenced by the 44% year-on-year drop in German automotive exports to China in 2025; squeezed margins for local companies, due in particular to significant production overcapacity; and less leeway for multinationals operating in the country. Andrew Bishop goes even further. "China is not only an economic threat to Europe. It is also the country that is currently enabling Russia to continue fighting in Ukraine. What if Beijing wants Moscow to emerge victorious from the conflict? China also poses a physical threat to Europe." This forces European leaders to perform a real balancing act. "It is essential to stabilise relations with Beijing. But we must be careful not to overplay the Chinese card," warns Agatha Kratz. The list of blows to American democracy grows longer almost every week: dismantling of countervailing powers, particularly judicial ones; recurrent criticism of the media and use of "fake news"; closures of federal agencies operating in the fields of the environment, public health, diversity and inclusion; electoral redistricting designed to favour the Republican Party. Not to mention the protesters killed by immigration police in suspicious circumstances. Since Donald J. Trump's return to the White House in January 2025, the foundations of democracy have been severely tested. "There has been an undeniable change of direction in this area," acknowledges Thomas Gomart. To the point of heralding a shift, in the more or less short term, to a more authoritarian regime? The geopolitical expert is reassuring. Unlike other countries, such as Russia, "the United States has a system of separation of powers, and civil society is mobilising" The imminent holding of crucial elections, in particular the midterm elections on 3 November, also presents a real opportunity for the federal government to "correct" these abuses, Thomas Gomart believes.
